existing_edge_1234.relationship: Settler against franchise colonialism: settler colonies 'were not primarily established to extract surplus value from indigenous labour' but 'premised on displacing indigenes from (or replacing them on) the land' (1999), 'a specific social formation' whose specificity is to be retained (2006)
existing_edge_1234.evidence_note: Wolfe 1999, pp. 1–2 (existing reading, cpl129_wolfe_1999_intro: the introduction distinguishes settler from franchise colonies) and p. 3 as quoted by Englert 2020 (read): "In contrast to the kind of colonial formation that Cabral or Fanon confronted settler colonies were not primarily established to extract surplus value from indigenous labour. Rather, they are premised on displacing indigenes from (or replacing them on) the land". Wolfe 2006 (read in full): "settler colonialism is a specific social formation and it is desirable to retain that specificity". Englert finds the Fanon/Algeria example contradictory (Algeria depended on Indigenous labour). A comparison, not a critique: Hoxie 2008 (existing abstract) places the frame inside postcolonial critique, while Veracini's claim that postcolonial studies missed the settler situation is drawn at entry level (edge_882 revised). (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

patrick_wolfe.relationship: Settler colonialism as 'a structure not an event': settler colonizers 'come to stay'; the form 'destroys to replace', is 'inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal', has territory as its 'irreducible element' and persists after the frontier as 'structural genocide' (1994–2006)
patrick_wolfe.evidence_note: Revision of 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md P.6, p4B_rel_01): the 2006 essay, read in full in the Internet Archive capture of the journal's free-to-read page (screq_wolfe_2006 addendum), joins the 1999 introduction (pp. 1–2, read earlier: settler colonies 'were (are) premised on the elimination of native societies'; 'invasion is a structure not an event'; contents and catalogue checked). Wolfe 2006, in his words: 'Settler colonialism is inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal' (p. 387, pages per Kauanui 2016); 'Territoriality is settler colonialism's specific, irreducible element'; 'settler colonizers come to stay: invasion is a structure not an event' (p. 388; his note 7 refers the formula to the 1999 book, p. 2, and to 'Nation and MiscegeNation', 1994, p. 96); 'Settler colonialism destroys to replace'; 'elimination refers to more than the summary liquidation of Indigenous people, though it includes that' (p. 390); 'settler colonialism is relatively impervious to regime change'; 'structural genocide' (p. 403). A contribution, not a founding: earlier settler-society studies (1983, 1995) and earlier usage (Veracini 2013; Kauanui 2016, note 7: Sayegh 1965, Rodinson 1973) precede it, and Kauanui records that Wolfe 'insisted … that he did not create the field of settler colonial studies—that Native scholars did'. The earlier note's Canadian PhD counts are moved to the entry's scope_note (user rule, 2026-10-23); bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

patrick_wolfe.relationship: A history of Victorian and Australian anthropology in its settler-colonial setting
patrick_wolfe.evidence_note: In-period evidence (1999). The contents page lists chapters on mother-right ('Sex and Property in Victorian Anthropology'), totemism ('Victorian Anthropology's Eternal Dichotomy') and E. B. Tylor ('Survival in a Paradigm Shift: E.B. Tylor and the Problem of the Text'), alongside virgin birth in anthropology and in Australian settler discourse. Catalogue subjects: Anthropology -- Australia -- History; Racism in anthropology -- Australia. Introduction p. 1 read: the book is 'a history not so much of anthropology itself as of its ideological entanglements'. The chapters' stance toward these anthropologists is not read here. If the introduction confirms a critical argument, a critique edge to anthropology/evolution may be the better reading. A historian's account of the discipline, not anthropological fieldwork. Addendum 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md P.6, p4B_rel_02): Veracini's obituary (read in full) reports that the 1999 book 'was ostensibly a history of Australian anthropology', that 'settler colonialism' was 'only added at the very end and at the request of the publisher', and that 'to explain the evolution of anthropology Patrick defined settler colonialism as distinct from colonialism'; Goeman (read in full) records Audra Simpson's memory of him as a historian 'of anthropology itself, and its relationship to politics'. The chapters remain unread, so the critique/contribution question stays open.

patrick_wolfe.relationship: A settler-colonial analytic worked out in conversation with Native American and Indigenous Studies: US Indian policy (removal, allotment, blood quantum, termination) read as successive modalities of elimination (2006, 2011); 'a key scholar in conceiving of a settler-colonial analytic in relation to Indigenous thinking' (Goeman, 2016)
patrick_wolfe.evidence_note: Goeman 2016 (read in full): "a key scholar in conceiving of a settler-colonial analytic in relation to Indigenous thinking and scholarship that exists far longer than settler nations"; "He critically engaged our field in a respectful and nuanced manner". Kauanui 2016 (read in full), note 7: "his long time, direct intellectual engagement with scholars in Native American and Indigenous Studies", and para. 2: he insisted "that Native scholars did" create the field. Wolfe 2006 (read in full), sections on discovery and preemption, the Cherokee removal, allotment, blood quantum ("statistical extermination", quoting Jaimes) and termination; "After the Frontier" (2011) is unread. A contribution to the conversation, not an origin: the entry's Indigenous methods are not derived from him, and the dissent of Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel (2014) is recorded on the entry. Replaces the former comparison row. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

patrick_wolfe.relationship: Race as the outcome of 'differentiation, which is an intensely conflictual process' (2001): 'a race cannot be taken as given. It is made in the targeting'; Black people 'racialized as slaves', Indians eliminated 'as Indians' (2006); a comparative typology of colonial race regimes in Traces of History (2016)
patrick_wolfe.evidence_note: Wolfe 2006 (read in full), opening section: "different racial regimes encode and reproduce the unequal relationships into which Europeans coerced the populations concerned"; "Black people's enslavement produced an inclusive taxonomy … For Indians, in stark contrast, non-Indian ancestry compromised their indigeneity"; "a race cannot be taken as given. It is made in the targeting"; and note 62 quoting his own 2001 essay, p. 894: "Difference … is not simply given. It is the outcome of differentiation, which is an intensely conflictual process." The 2001 essay is otherwise unread (Crossref: AHR 106:3, June 2001). Traces of History (2016) known through the British Library contents note (chapters on Australia, the United States, central Europe, Brazil, Palestine) and Veracini's obituary (read): it "utilises his analysis of racism under settler colonialism in order to explain racism everywhere else" and provides "a compelling typology of racial formations". Strengthens the entry-level comparison edge_885, which stays. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

patrick_wolfe.relationship: Settler colonialism set beside genocide studies: the Holocaust as 'the non-paradigmatic paradigm' against which 'qualified genocides' are devalued; 'structural genocide' proposed to retain settler colonialism's specificity without 'hierarchy among victims'; a chapter in Moses's Empire, Colony, Genocide (2006–08)
patrick_wolfe.evidence_note: Wolfe 2006 (read in full): "Settler colonialism is inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal"; "The best known of all genocides was internal to Europe"; Lemkin's definition (note 6); Hull, Pohl, Zimmerer and "the modernity of colonialism"; "the Holocaust, the non-paradigmatic paradigm that, being the indispensable example, can never merely exemplify"; "the term 'structural genocide' avoids the questions of degree—and, therefore, of hierarchy among victims" (p. 403 per Kauanui). The 2008 chapter in Moses ed. is unread (Berghahn contents; Docker's "Are Settler-Colonies Inherently Genocidal?" in the same volume). The holocaust entry is historiographical; this compares frames and does not claim he wrote Holocaust history. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

patrick_wolfe.relationship: Settler against franchise colonialism: settler colonies 'were not primarily established to extract surplus value from indigenous labour' but 'premised on displacing indigenes from (or replacing them on) the land' (1999), 'a specific social formation' whose specificity is to be retained (2006)
patrick_wolfe.evidence_note: Wolfe 1999, pp. 1–2 (existing reading, cpl129_wolfe_1999_intro: the introduction distinguishes settler from franchise colonies) and p. 3 as quoted by Englert 2020 (read): "In contrast to the kind of colonial formation that Cabral or Fanon confronted settler colonies were not primarily established to extract surplus value from indigenous labour. Rather, they are premised on displacing indigenes from (or replacing them on) the land". Wolfe 2006 (read in full): "settler colonialism is a specific social formation and it is desirable to retain that specificity". Englert finds the Fanon/Algeria example contradictory (Algeria depended on Indigenous labour). A comparison, not a critique: Hoxie 2008 (existing abstract) places the frame inside postcolonial critique, while Veracini's claim that postcolonial studies missed the settler situation is drawn at entry level (edge_882 revised). (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

patrick_wolfe.relationship: Treaties, preemption, removal and allotment read as 'the logic of elimination' rather than as relations and encounter: 'the murderous activities of the frontier rabble constitute [the colonial state's] principal means of expansion' (2006); set against the fur-trade historiography's 'middle ground', which Veracini records as a rival recovery (2013)
patrick_wolfe.evidence_note: Wolfe 2006 (read in full), second section (the doctrine of discovery, preemption, the Cherokee removal: "The American right to buy always superseded the Indian right not to sell" (Rosenthal, quoted); "Rather than something separate from or running counter to the colonial state, the murderous activities of the frontier rabble constitute its principal means of expansion") and sixth section (allotment, blood quantum, termination). Veracini 2013, concluding section (author manuscript, read): "the recovery of a long lasting 'middle ground' between indigenous and settler polities in the past, sustained the possibility of renewed relationships"; "both the Canadian and US historiographies were late in adopting settler colonialism as a category of analysis". edge_869 already compares the two fields; this names the person's own reading. Canadian material is not his. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

patrick_wolfe.relationship: Wolfe took from Harris the sentence that 'the principal momentum of settler colonialism comes into focus' when capital's interest in uncluttered access to land is combined with settlers' interest in land as livelihood (2004, quoted 2006): a use as evidence, moderate
patrick_wolfe.evidence_note: Wolfe 2006 (read in full), third section and note 36, quoting Harris, "How Did Colonialism Dispossess?" (2004), p. 179: "Combine capital's interest in uncluttered access to land and settlers' interest in land as livelihood, and the principal momentum of settler colonialism comes into focus." Englert 2020 (read) also uses Harris 2004, p. 172, against Wolfe. The direction matters for edge_1014, which found no derivation of Harris from Wolfe: the citation runs the other way. A single quotation; influence in the sense of a use as evidence, as for locB_rel_26 in revision 1.152. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

patrick_wolfe.relationship: Critiques address both Wolfe's model and its subsequent uses: Macoun and Strakosch question structural inevitability; Rowse questions a teleology of elimination; Englert directly challenges elimination as the defining logic. Kauanui defends Wolfe against formulaic citation while rejecting the replacement of Indigenous Studies (2013–20)
patrick_wolfe.evidence_note: Macoun and Strakosch 2013 (author version, read): "SCT can depict colonization as structurally inevitable"; "Foundational scholar Patrick Wolfe has been labelled 'very much a structuralist stuck in a poststructuralist world'"; "a kind of colonial fatalism"; "it does not account for Indigenous lives". Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel 2014 (read): "treating settler colonialism as a meta-structure, thus erasing both its contingency and the dynamics that co-constitute" it. Rowse 2014 (abstract, existing): a "teleology of elimination". Kauanui 2016 (read in full): a criticism of Wolfe's reception rather than of Wolfe, defending the theory against the phrase that 'often seems to stand-in for a serious engagement' with it, and asking that "Settler Colonial Studies does not, should not, and cannot replace Indigenous Studies". 'Wolfe and his Indigenous critics' is the citation graph's category for a co-citation pairing, not every author's declared position (Sol review 1.156, finding 3). Englert 2020 (read in full): "a critique of the Wolfe-an model"; elimination "does not accurately define the overall logic of settler colonialism, as claimed by Wolfe". Fairness: Kauanui and Goeman record his disclaimers and his engagement with NAIS; Macoun and Strakosch call his contribution "vital". (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

patrick_wolfe.relationship: Wolfe explicitly agrees that frontier closure marks a major change, interpreting the post-frontier shift through Indigenous containment and assimilation within continuing settler colonialism (2013).
patrick_wolfe.evidence_note: Primary 257–259, especially 258, and 276 n 19. Qualified agreement is not blanket defense or proved influence. This remains an undirected comparison/reception link; Native sovereignty and continuing elimination remain central to Wolfe’s different account.

patrick_wolfe.relationship: Wolfe uses O’Brien’s evidence on New England treaty status and earlier blood-quantum practices in his history of Indigenous racialization and dispossession.
patrick_wolfe.evidence_note: Own fresh selected 2016 body and actual endnotes: chapter 5/n30 uses Firsting 203 for disadvantages facing tribes dispossessed before US treaty relationships; chapter 6/n92 uses Firsting 128 for an earlier Connecticut blood-quantum example. These are two specific resources within one pair/kind, not evidence that O’Brien endorsed Wolfe’s entire comparative framework. O’Brien’s cited pages remain unread in full; Wolfe’s original legal/historical sources are not independently checked. Ebook PDF pagination is explicit and not passed off as print pages.

patrick_wolfe.relationship: With Denise Henning (2021), Wheeler adopts Wolfe's definition: in the Americas 'classic colonialism evolved into settler colonialism', whose goal 'is the erasure of Indigenous peoples in order to establish settler rights to Indigenous lands and resources (Wolfe, 2006)'.
patrick_wolfe.evidence_note: Henning and Wheeler, New Directions for Student Services 2020, nos. 171–172 (online 30 April 2021), section 'Colonization and intergenerational trauma' (early-view p. 3; print pp. 57–67); Wolfe 2006 (Journal of Genocide Research 8:4) in the references. A co-authored study (Henning first author) of rural Indigenous students' postsecondary experience: it uses the frame as historical context and does not discuss settler colonial studies as a field. Her earlier colonial analysis used Blauner's colonial model (1998) and postcolonial and anti-colonial theory (2000, 2010), without settler-colonial vocabulary.

patrick_wolfe.relationship: Wolfe uses Jacobson’s formulation of republican inclusion and racial/gender exclusion as interdependent to develop his account of race and colonial power.
patrick_wolfe.evidence_note: Own Wolfe 2001, 875/n29 quotes Jacobson 22–23 while discussing Morgan’s slavery/freedom analysis; Morgan and David Brion Davis retain separate substantive credit. Wolfe adds a specific reservation about Jacobson’s treatment of liberalism, and 893/n100 includes him among resources for the historical expansion of whiteness while preserving differences from anti-Black racialization. Positive use coexists with the separate qualification; original Jacobson 22–23 not freshly read, so the quotation’s mediation through Wolfe is explicit.

patrick_wolfe.relationship: Wolfe qualifies Jacobson’s account of republican inclusion and exclusion for leaving liberalism’s own credentials insufficiently interrogated.
patrick_wolfe.evidence_note: Own 875/n29 explicitly attaches this limited reservation to his otherwise substantive quotation of Whiteness 22–23. This is a brief, scoped critical qualification, not an extended refutation of Jacobson’s book or a claim he ignored all relations of power. Wolfe’s positive use remains separately represented; his 893/n100 distinction among racial regimes is not falsely treated as refuting Jacobson’s own 9 warning against equating experiences. Original Jacobson 22–23 remains unread here.

patrick_wolfe.relationship: Invokes Wolfe’s call for a unified historical field while arguing that representation and material consequences should be studied together (2003).
patrick_wolfe.evidence_note: Own introduction 10–11 explicitly uses Wolfe in defending the combination of political, administrative, military, social and cultural history. This does not automatically classify the book as adopting every settler-colonial model. Note 28’s body and the Wolfe original are unread; exact title or edition not invented.

patrick_wolfe.relationship: Carter uses Wolfe’s logic-of-elimination framework when interpreting the dispossession and exclusion underlying prairie homesteading.
patrick_wolfe.evidence_note: Imperial Plots 6/note 6 explicitly names Wolfe and applies the formulation within her analysis of land, reserves and excluded Indigenous farmers. The note cites his 2006 Journal of Genocide Research article, 387; the bibliography supplies 387–409. The article remains unread in this dossier. This is a bounded resource in the 2016 book, read in its corrected 2018 reprint, not an influence inferred from citation alone or a retrospective classification of all Carter’s earlier work. Earlier edge_1315 retains its limits.

patrick_wolfe.relationship: Greer adopts Wolfe’s critique of naturalized settler history and continuing dispossession while seeking a more differentiated colonial chronology.
patrick_wolfe.evidence_note: Own 2019:62–63 explicitly calls for taking on board Wolfe’s historiographical critique, developed further by Veracini, and values the structure-not-event formulation. Notes 2–3 and 7–8 distinguish Wolfe 2007,1999,2006 and Veracini 2010; originals remain unread here. Positive uptake coexists with Greer’s scope objection; neither automatic full agreement nor a direct personal teaching relationship is inferred.

patrick_wolfe.relationship: Greer argues that Wolfe’s settlement–exploitation dyad needs extension to capture other overlapping colonial forms in northern North America.
patrick_wolfe.evidence_note: Own 2019:63–64 names Wolfe’s Australia/India focus, then introduces imperial/commercial penetration and extractivism as additional modes. Greer insists these coexist and overlap rather than form self-contained stages. He expressly values Wolfe’s critique and does not attribute every casual temporal flattening to Wolfe himself. Existing group critique edge_1012 remains; original Wolfe texts are unread.

patrick_wolfe.relationship: Wolfe adapts Mauss’s total social phenomenon to analyse anthropology as a total discursive practice participating in colonial settlement.
patrick_wolfe.evidence_note: Own 1999 introduction 3 explicitly identifies the adaptation, while note 6 quotes Mauss 1925 [1970]:1 on simultaneously religious, legal, moral, economic, aesthetic and morphological institutions. Wolfe treats anthropological debates as primary data rather than adjudicating their claims about Indigenous life. This is a particular methodological resource, not equivalence between the two complete projects or a newly read Mauss original; bracketed 1970 does not become first publication.

patrick_wolfe.relationship: Wolfe uses Spivak’s distinction between exposing mechanisms and making individuals speak to explain his refusal of ethnographic ventriloquism.
patrick_wolfe.evidence_note: Own introduction 4 invokes Spivak 1988:288 while distinguishing the analysis of anthropological constructions from an attempt to recuperate an allegedly pristine Indigenous voice behind them. Political and empirical methodological limits converge in his argument. This records his explicit use of a particular distinction, not proof he adopted all of Spivak’s work, a claim Indigenous people had no voice, or a newly read Spivak original; the cited original title is not guessed.

patrick_wolfe.relationship: Chakrabarty supervised and commented on the entire doctoral draft from which substantial portions of Wolfe’s first book developed.
patrick_wolfe.evidence_note: Own acknowledgments vii distinguish three successive supervisors, Maurice Bloch, Greg Dening and finally Chakrabarty; the last read and commented on the whole draft. This is specific critical scholarly input to the thesis, not a claim he alone formed Wolfe or read the final 1999 book. Wolfe explicitly separates the later rewritten book and the whole-book readings by Phillip Darby and Michele Grossman. No particular adopted revision or common theoretical doctrine is invented.

fanon.relationship: contributes analyses of colonial domination and liberation
fanon.evidence_note: Psychiatric inquiry and liberation politics intersect without defining all anti-colonial history. The checked 1961 passages criticize elite succession and stress participation; Fanon’s regional and gendered claims remain open to criticism.

fanon.relationship: Fanon becomes a named resource in Chakrabarty’s account of colonialism and humanism
fanon.evidence_note: Later reception is selective; anti-colonial struggle and postcolonial scholarship are not interchangeable. Later postcolonial theory takes up Fanon selectively; psychiatry, race, and political strategy should not be collapsed. The primary 2000 introduction, p. 5, supplies one documented uptake. Bhabha’s Fanon chapter is a further bibliographic lead, not yet a passage check.

fanon.relationship: provides psychoanalytic resources reworked in an analysis of racialized colonial experience
fanon.evidence_note: Fanon explicitly discusses Freud in the 1952 introduction, extending explanation from individual development to sociogeny. Psychoanalysis remains one resource among several; this does not place Fanon within psychohistory or imply unchanged application.

fanon.relationship: Fanon distinguishes popular emancipation from elite succession
fanon.evidence_note: His 1961 criticism of the intermediary national bourgeoisie and emphasis on political participation supply an earlier conceptual resource for studying nationalism. This is an editorial connection, not demonstrated influence on every later nationalism theorist.

fanon.relationship: Hall uses Fanon to connect historical recovery with colonial dispossession and changing identity
fanon.evidence_note: Hall’s primary pp. 223–226 name Fanon’s national-culture and colonizing-experience arguments. The contribution concerns this specific diasporic identity discussion, not a genealogy of all identity histories.

fanon.relationship: Fanon’s claim that colonialism shaped the colonizers as much as the colonized frames the question of how empire was lived “at home” (2002–2003)
fanon.evidence_note: Her own statement, read by the second research pass (JBS 42:4, 2003, p. 530): "Yet if, as Frantz Fanon argued, colonialism shaped the colonizers as much as the colonized then how was this expressed in everyday culture? How was it lived 'at home' as well as in the empire?" One explicit sentence framing the project; the Fanon text is not specified. Not to be confused with edge_418 (fanon → identity), which concerns Stuart Hall.

fanon.relationship: As Gonzalez, Modzelewski, Panich and Schneider explain, Wilson credits Fanon’s writing on decolonization with helping her articulate her own struggle in Reclaiming Our Humanity (2004).
fanon.evidence_note: Explicitly mediated through the four named authors’ substantive 2006 account, read in an institutional repository. They also credit Paulo Freire’s work on praxis; his contribution is not reassigned to Fanon. Wilson’s original 2004 chapter remains unread here, and her family and community sources of knowledge retain their independent standing.

fanon.relationship: As Deborah Simmons interprets his work, Adams draws on Fanon’s account of decolonization to connect autobiographical experiences of colonial alienation with collective historical struggle.
fanon.evidence_note: Explicitly mediated through Simmons’s 2002 tribute, pp. 6–7. Her reading connects Prison of Grass and Tortured People; their original and revised editions remain distinct. This is a specified intellectual resource, not an inference from Adams’s Marxist politics. The complete book bodies remain unread here.

fanon.relationship: Byrnes and Coleborne identify Fanon as an intellectual resource for Walker’s counter-history of colonization and analysis of colonial power and resistance.
fanon.evidence_note: This is the explicitly named reading of Giselle Byrnes and Catharine Coleborne in their joint 2011 editorial: p. 8 discusses colonial disavowal, and note 48 names the revised 2004 Ka Whawhai Tonu Mātou and Fanon’s The Wretched of the Earth and Black Skin, White Masks. Walker’s book and these Fanon editions were not freshly read. The 2004 witness is not silently backdated to the 1990 original or treated as the sole origin of Māori historiography.

fanon.relationship: Includes Fanon in the political reading through which he developed his approach to Black self-determination and Marxist history.
fanon.evidence_note: Kelley’s answers describe reading Fanon in an All-African People’s Revolutionary Party study group, alongside Nkrumah, Ture, Cabral and Marx. The named-resources answer situates these readings in his effort to connect self-determination, political economy and more than material conditions. No particular Fanon title, formal teacher or exclusive influence is invented; original works unread.

fanon.relationship: Finds at Kahnawà:ke no 'doubleness' of colonised consciousness of the kind 'that Fanon, Bhabha and Giddens speak of', but 'a tripleness, a quadrupleness' revealed at the point of refusal (2007)
fanon.evidence_note: Own words, 2007, p. 74. Nicoll (2015, p. 56, read) independently reports that 'Simpson distinguishes this refusal from Fanonian "double consciousness"'. A qualified critique of one concept, not of Fanon's work as a whole. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md)

fanon.relationship: Coulthard uses Fanon's critique of Hegel's master–slave dialectic against liberal recognition, while holding that Fanon's self-recognition 'fails to push us far enough' in settler states (2009)
fanon.evidence_note: Own words, dissertation pp. 25–27 (Fanon used against Hegel and liberal recognition) and p. 159: Fanon's notion of self-recognition 'remains an innovative and important contribution', but he was 'less willing to explore the role that these forms might play in providing substantive alternatives'. Influence with explicit qualification. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md) Locators corrected in revision 1.204 to the printed page numbers of the UVic PDF (rechecked 2026-10-28, data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-B.md).

fanon.relationship: Takes Fanon and Memmi as 'the classic sources' on internalised colonisation, while noting that The Wretched of the Earth does not treat Native North Americans (1999)
fanon.evidence_note: Own words, 1999 dissertation (read 2026-10-28): PDF p. 48, 'Frantz Fanon and Albert Memmi are the classic sources for discussion on the processes of internalization'; PDF p. 12, classic (Fanon, Memmi) and contemporary works 'have convincingly shown that colonization produces a pervasive structural and psychological relationship between the colonizer and the colonized'; PDF p. 40 (qualification), 'Frantz Fanon in Wretched of the Earth does not deal with the treatment of Native North Americans either'. Parallel to edge_2140 (Said). Memmi has no node. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-C.md)

fanon.relationship: Chukwudinma and Kallon trace Rodney’s early use of Fanon’s analysis of the national bourgeoisie when interpreting Tanzania’s socialist experiment.
fanon.evidence_note: Named scholarly readers Chukwudinma and Kallon 2025 explicitly identify The Pitfalls of National Consciousness as Rodney’s frequently invoked resource during 1969–74 and afterwards. They quote his 1972 accounts of the dependent petty bourgeoisie and intelligentsia’s possible transformation, while distinguishing his terminology from Fanon’s and crediting Cabral for a class-suicide formulation Rodney associated with Fanon. The authors show later revision and continuing debt rather than an unchanging or exclusive lineage. This is their attributed analysis of quoted published and archival Rodney material; the original papers, full lectures and Fanon book remain unread.

fanon.relationship: Chukwudinma and Kallon identify Rodney’s later disagreements with Fanon over revolutionary organization and the class character of postcolonial African societies.
fanon.evidence_note: The authors’ 2025 original article quotes Rodney’s 1973 Cabral eulogy and 1978 Hamburg distinction between violence itself and its political organization, then traces his post-1974 view of Tanzania’s bureaucracy as a ruling class rooted in production. They describe a move beyond the early model of a dependent stratum that might renounce privilege. Their account expressly calls Rodney’s portrayal of Fanon as an apostle of spontaneity a misreading, since Fanon also demanded organization; it also finds that Rodney retained some Fanonian hopes about guerrilla leadership. The disagreement is Rodney’s interpretation as mediated by these two readers, not a finding that Fanon simply ignored organization or a complete rejection of Fanon. Original eulogy, recordings, research papers and Fanon book unread. The existing James 401 criticism concerns a distinct retrospective assessment of Rodney.

mariana_valverde.relationship: Moral regulation as the formation of ethical subjectivity, carried out by philanthropies, churches and professions as well as the state: social purity in English Canada, 1885–1925 (1991–92; the 1988 article with Weir is listed but unread)
mariana_valverde.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements. 'Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State', Labour/Le Travail 30 (1992), pp. 213–222, read in full: 'I have argued elsewhere that the discourse of moral reform needs to be analyzed seriously, not merely dismissed as a cover for class interests', though 'moral discourse does as a matter of contingent fact legitimize certain class, gender, and racial interests' (p. 216); she credits Corrigan and Sayer's The Great Arch with pioneering 'the liberal state's role in constituting subjectivities' (p. 217). The Age of Light, Soap, and Water (1991) is known here through in-period reviewers' quotations and through Google Books search-within snippets of the 2008 University of Toronto Press reissue (volume ghqEyXf5950C; partial preview, page images not viewable here because the viewing limit was reached), which keep the 1991 pagination: reformers sought 'to reshape the ethical subjectivity of both immigrants and native-born Canadians' (p. 17; quoted by Dehli 1992, p. 316); purity work 'was not simply a question of banning obscene books or suppressing prostitution but was rather a campaign to educate the next generation' (p. 17; quoted by McCormick 1992, p. 124); the reform movements 'helped to shape the bourgeoisie, which led the movements, as well as the working class' (p. 15; Dehli, p. 318); 'Moral regulation is very closely linked to state formation, as the British school of historical sociology has argued; but as Foucault and his followers have pointed out, the state has no monopoly on moral regulation' (p. 165; snippet, the last clause also quoted by Dehli, p. 317); '[m]oral regulation is an important aspect of ruling, helping to constitute class, gender, sexual, and race relations' (p. 166, as quoted by Wright 1995, p. 124). Her notes, seen only as snippets, place the concept: in The Great Arch 'the role of the state in moral regulation is highlighted, and their theorization has been influential here; but the agencies of regulation internal to civil society are obscured' (n. 34, p. 171); Corrigan and Sayer 'do not differentiate between moral and other modes of social regulation; by contrast, I restrict the term to mean the formation of ethical subjectivity' (p. 173). Note 33 (p. 171) cites the 1988 article with Lorna Weir, which is unread here. In-period reception by historians. Tina Loo (Labour/Le Travail 30, 1992, pp. 277–279, read) calls the book 'a provocative and valuable contribution to the history of social reform and, more significantly, because of its self-conscious use of theory, to the writing of Canadian history' (p. 279). Donald Wright (Acadiensis, 1995, pp. 122–126 read) calls it a 'much talked about treatise' by 'a sociologist' (p. 122) and its concept of 'slippages' among class, gender, sexuality and race her 'most original' contribution (p. 124). Carolyn Strange and Tina Loo's Making Good: Law and Moral Regulation in Canada (1997; Google Books snippets, pp. 5, 63) write that 'Theorists influenced by philosopher Michel Foucault have urged scholars to abandon the social-control model for a more flexible concept of regulation' (p. 5) and cite 'Mariana Valverde and others' on prostitution as 'the social evil' (p. 63). Mary Louise Adams's 'In Sickness and in Health: State Formation, Moral Regulation, and Early VD Initiatives in Ontario' (1994) is cited at title level only. In-period criticism. Loo finds the second argument, on philanthropy and the state, 'more asserted than proved' (p. 279). Kari Dehli (Historical Studies in Education, 1992, pp. 315–319, read) would draw 'not quite so sharply drawn' conclusions about state and civil society and finds that she moves 'quickly from analysis of discursive strategies ... to drawing conclusions about people's motives and intentions' (pp. 318–319). Wright judges her claim that audiences 'knew precisely what was meant' 'untenable' and finds 'the impoverished immigrant and the "fallen woman" ... conspicuously silent', so that 'the silence of the consumer amidst the din of the producer gives the impression of top-down social control, precisely what Valverde sought to avoid' (pp. 125–126). Chris McCormick (Atlantis, 1992, pp. 123–125, read) asks how her interpretations are made and judges that a 'thorough' reading of context is 'optimistic' (p. 123), while agreeing that 'Regulation is a better word than control' (p. 124). Sociologists reformulated the concept: Alan Hunt's 1997 abstract (read) treats moral regulation not as 'a specific moral arena' but as 'a component of all fields of social relations', a wider definition than hers; in Governing Morals (1999; snippets) he writes 'I do not take issue with Valverde's invocation of ethical subjectivity, but I emphasise the mundane features of self-governing' (p. 155). Dean (1994) and Ruonavaara (1997) are cited through their abstracts as on the moral_regulation node. A contribution, not a founding: Corrigan (1981) and Corrigan and Sayer (1985) precede her, and she credits them. Diseases of the Will (1998), on alcohol and the governance of the will, is title-level here (snippets only) and does not support this edge.

mariana_valverde.relationship: Protestant reformers read as moral regulators rather than as religious actors, and the church historians' objection that this excised the churches from progressive thought (1991–96)
mariana_valverde.evidence_note: Her object overlaps the field's. The book studies Methodist and Presbyterian church organizations, the Salvation Army, the WCTU, the YWCA and the National Council of Women (Dehli 1992, p. 316, read), with familiar reformers such as Chown, Shearer and Woodsworth (Loo 1992, p. 277, read). Her reading is regulatory: purity work 'was rather a campaign to educate the next generation' (p. 17, quoted by McCormick 1992, p. 124), and the discourse of moral reform 'needs to be analyzed seriously, not merely dismissed as a cover for class interests' ('Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State', 1992, p. 216, read). In-period objections from historians of religion and reform. Loo (Labour/Le Travail 30, 1992, p. 278, read) finds that 'religion and sectarian differences' get 'rather short shrift', suggests Richard Allen's typology of radical, progressive and conservative reformers, and holds that 'any discussion of the discourse of moral reform in Canada needs to address Christianity and certainly Protestantism more fully, even if only to dismiss its importance'. Nancy Christie and Michael Gauvreau, A Full-Orbed Christianity (1996), known here only through Google Books search-within snippets: 'historians such as Doug Owram and Mariana Valverde have adhered to a caricature of the antiquated and esoteric Victorian theologue to excise the churches from "progressive" currents of modern thought and social action' (p. xiii); 'Valverde has argued that in early twentieth-century Canada issues such as social purity and immigration were controlled by a hegemonic exercise of power by the state and middle-class organizations' (p. 187), and her analysis 'wrongly posits the view that given the hegemonic influence of the state, there was only one option regarding immigration policy – that of racism and the annihilation of immigrant culture', against which they set 'three divergent strands of opinion on the immigration question' among Protestant clergy (p. 188; n. 95, p. 328, cites her pp. 15, 112, 123–8). Their p. 187 summary attributes to her a state-centred hegemony that her own p. 165 qualifies ('the state has no monopoly on moral regulation'); the disagreement is recorded, not adjudicated. A comparison, as her roster row and edge_861 (moral_regulation – cdn_religion_reform) have it: the criticism runs from the church historians to her, and she did not answer it in a text read here. The dispute is person-level, which is why it is drawn from her entry; edge_861 stays the field-level comparison.

mariana_valverde.relationship: Liberalism read as a system of moral regulation and the liberal state as a constitutor of subjectivities (1991–92), beside the liberal order framework's later history of property, the individual and rule
mariana_valverde.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements, before McKay's prospectus (2000). 'Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State', Labour/Le Travail 30 (1992), pp. 213–222, read in full, endorses Mitchell Dean's argument 'that classical English liberalism was not a negation of state regulation but rather a particular system of economic, social, and moral regulation', so that 'a history of pauperism is also a genealogy of liberalism' (p. 217). She reviews Jean-Marie Fecteau's Un nouvel ordre des choses (1989) as 'a landmark work' whose 'theoretical sophistication' crosses 'the traditional historiographical boundaries separating coercion from benevolence and the state as a whole from charity' (pp. 221–222), but faults its 'moyens de contrôle' as 'a rather functionalist formulation', a 'model of negative class power', and adds that 'These moral codes are not intrinsic to the logic of capital, since capitalism works quite efficiently in different cultural systems' (p. 222). Note 10 (p. 220) cites Fecteau's essay in Greer and Radforth's Colonial Leviathan (1992), and the essay thanks Allan Greer for comments on a draft (p. 222). In the 1991 book (Google Books search-within snippets of the 2008 reissue, 1991 pagination) note 35 (p. 171) cites Bruce Curtis's 'Preconditions of the Canadian State', and she writes that moral regulation 'might be an important social process, which is intertwined with but is not an effect of either the economic or the political' (p. 165) and that 'one has to be sceptical of any claims that envision a clear separation between moral and economic regulation' (p. 166). Reviewers read the book's state argument in the same terms: private philanthropy 'allowed liberal democratic states to adhere to their policy of non-interference in the private sphere' (Loo 1992, p. 278, her paraphrase). Comparison only. The user decided (2026-10-12) that the liberal order framework is 'a different project closer to history of capitalism'; Fecteau and Curtis are shared ground (state formation), not membership. No in-period text by the framework's authors discussing her was read here (McKay's 2000 prospectus is paywalled and unread). edge_848 (liberal_order_framework – moral_regulation) is the field-level comparison. This edge is an editorial comparison of her 1992 argument with the later framework (McKay, 2000); she did not distinguish herself from a framework not yet formulated.

mariana_valverde.relationship: Scott's poststructuralist programme criticised by a sympathetic reader, who suggested that it may exaggerate what Foucault and Derrida can do for historians, for passing over discourse analysis's bias towards 'the sociology of domination', and (1995) for setting theory against working-class history
mariana_valverde.evidence_note: Her own in-period words (1990 essay read in full; 1995 essay, pp. 329–332 read). 'Poststructuralist Gender Historians: Are We Those Names?', Labour/Le Travail 25 (1990), pp. 227–236, reviews Scott's Gender and the Politics of History with Denise Riley's 'Am I That Name?'. She grants that Scott's approach 'has much to commend it' but finds her four elements of gender 'somewhat arbitrary' and asks whether the definition 'finally succeeds in transcending the idealism/materialism dichotomy' (p. 230). Scott's case studies show limitations 'symptomatic of the general limitations of discourse analysis as it has been used by social historians (myself included!)' (p. 231): there is 'an inherent bias in discourse analysis in favour of what some call "the sociology of domination." This problem, not discussed by Scott, does not discredit or make redundant discourse analysis' (p. 232). Scott's 'rather polemical book tends to sing the praises of discourse analysis without mentioning many of its problems', with a 'grandiose claim made by Scott on Foucault's behalf' (p. 232), and 'It may be that she exaggerates the contribution Foucault and Derrida can make to historical work' (p. 233). She ends that 'Scott's work deserves to be carefully read even by those who find some of its more polemical claims hard to swallow' (p. 233). 'Deconstructive Marxism', Labour/Le Travail 36 (1995), pp. 329–340 (pp. 329–332 read), sharpens the judgment: Scott 'made an influential attempt to extend the reach of deconstruction within historical writing to the certainties of class. Her argument was limited in many ways' (pp. 331–332); 'Scott probably used her new-found theories to justify a break with Marxism that she, like so many other former leftists on both sides of the Atlantic, wanted to make anyway', and 'the book undoubtedly made an important contribution to the feminist analysis of both politics and history: but it did so, or at least gave the appearance of doing so, at the expense of working-class history' (p. 332). She criticises the other side too: 'for many labour historians, any hint of theoretical sophistication became prima faciae evidence of political backsliding' (p. 332), and her note names Bryan Palmer's Descent into Discourse as 'the by now standard Marxist critique of Scott' (p. 332, n. 5). edge_891 (joan_wallach_scott → cdn_women_gender) already cites the 1990 essay as evidence of Canadian engagement with Scott; this edge records her own criticism of Scott's position, which edge_891 does not carry. A critique within broad sympathy, not a rejection: the qualifications above are part of the claim.

mariana_valverde.relationship: Sangster questions Valverde’s suggestion that women’s history is not self-sufficient, reading it as implying gender history’s superiority (1996).
mariana_valverde.evidence_note: The attribution is explicit in p. 240 n3; this records Sangster’s reading, not an agreed hierarchy.

(2016), 174 and178, expressly identifies her Foucauldian working tradition and uses power/knowledge to explain how jurisdiction assigns different forms of governance. Her adoption of Bakhtin is explicitly an additional resource rather than abandonment of Foucault, while she rejects automatic eclecticism. mariana_valverde.relationship: Valverde uses Derrida’s Spectres of Marx to challenge the opposition between theoretical sophistication and politically engaged labour history.
mariana_valverde.evidence_note: Own Deconstructive Marxism (1995),332–338, calls the book a resource for rethinking the theory/politics and ideal/material oppositions, while preserving Marx’s emancipatory project and the importance of historical inheritance. Her339–340 discussion explicitly stops short of Derrida’s undeconstructible justice and expresses reservations about its mystical context. mariana_valverde.relationship: McKay challenges the extension of Valverde’s Toronto–Ottawa evidence into an undifferentiated English Canada while praising her methodological innovation.
mariana_valverde.evidence_note: Own A Note on Region (2000), 92–93 and note 3, names The Age of Light, Soap and Water and questions its spatial scale, regional typicality and use of a part to stand for a whole. He calls the book pioneering and deserving of praise for its methodology, while suggesting that a Boston–Halifax axis might be more pertinent for some Atlantic questions. This is a specific geographical and historiographical objection, not rejection of moral regulation or a new reading of Valverde’s complete book. The article lightly edits an unpresented 1997 talk and is dated by its 2000 publication; Valverde’s earlier work is not treated as responding to McKay’s later framework.

tzvetan_todorov.relationship: Uses conquest as a historical case for examining attitudes toward other societies
tzvetan_todorov.evidence_note: The three authored opening paragraphs of “The Morality of Conquest, ” printed 89, explicitly identify the conquest of Mexico and its texts as the case. This limited methodological connection does not assert the unread book’s full thesis or label Todorov a member of a later school.

tzvetan_todorov.relationship: Challenges the assumption that remembering victimhood necessarily prevents violence
tzvetan_todorov.evidence_note: Own UNESCO essay distinguishes selective remembrance from ethical use and warns that former victims can become aggressors. This is his bounded intervention on public memory, not a psychological finding or a universal judgment on victims.

tzvetan_todorov.relationship: Pagden adopts Todorov’s contrast between Spanish initiative and Mexica efforts to maintain the status quo in his particular interpretation of the first sustained encounter, and acknowledges Todorov’s suggestions for improving his work.
tzvetan_todorov.evidence_note: Pagden’s introduction, p. lv and note 43, explicitly identifies Todorov’s point; acknowledgments p. vi credit Todorov alongside Richard Kagan and Ángel Delgado Gómez. This is a scoped use and named feedback, not endorsement of every part of Todorov’s conquest thesis or a general claim about Indigenous passivity. Hernán Cortés is the letters’ author; Pagden is translator, editor and introduction author; J. H. Elliott’s introductory essay is separate. Pages were read in the 2001 Yale Nota Bene edition of a work first published in 1971 and revised in 1986. tzvetan_todorov.relationship: Todorov credits Barthes’s receptive teaching and intellectual exchanges with amplifying students’ ideas during his early French literary formation.
tzvetan_todorov.evidence_note: Own1997P11 describes admiration, theoretical humility and active improvement of students’ ideas, not merely thesis supervision. P15 says Barthes’s works played an important role while distinguishing Todorov’s later truth-regulated dialogue from what he thinks Barthes would share. Genette/Bremond/Metz network retains shared credit. Spanish interview rendering/translator unestablished; no complete Barthes originals read.

tzvetan_todorov.relationship: Todorov recalls Lévi-Strauss’s clear rational argument and movement between detailed analysis and bold generalization as an admired model in his structuralist formation.
tzvetan_todorov.evidence_note: Own 2001 reply in 2003 translated sample footer 8 praises precisely these qualities while saying personal contact was rare and kinship/myth studies differed from his literary interests. It also qualifies later scientific ambitions and relativism. Admired intellectual model, not direct mentorship, wholesale allegiance or claim all remembered reading was contemporaneous. La Pensée sauvage 1962/Anthropologie structurale 1958 identified by notes 13–14, original bodies unread.

tzvetan_todorov.relationship: Todorov questions Lévi-Strauss’s sweeping scientific ambitions and some claims about cultural relativism and the subject, while retaining admiration for his analytical reasoning.
tzvetan_todorov.evidence_note: Own translated retrospective footer 8 explicitly recalls a critical study later included in Nous et les autres and states that peremptory claims seemed to exceed Lévi-Strauss’s own best thought. Not a report that Lévi-Strauss replied: Todorov says there was no reaction. Exact underlying chapter and full original anthropological works unread. Source is 2001 interview/2003 Spanish edition, not a falsely contemporaneous 1960s objection.

tzvetan_todorov.relationship: Todorov identifies Weber’s ideal types and analyses as attractive resources within his renewed study of political philosophy for Nous et les autres.
tzvetan_todorov.evidence_note: Own1997P21 distinguishes useful reading from agreement with every author. It names Strauss’s natural-right dispute and Aron’s introduction as surrounding interpretive mediation, then explicitly states attraction to Weber’s ideal types/analyses. Max Weber, not Eugen Weber. Cited original works unread; no assertion all political-philosophical reading had one source or first-reading date.

tzvetan_todorov.relationship: Todorov resists Weber’s agonistic account of war and the ultimate incompatibility of values, preferring dialogue and a horizon of universality.
tzvetan_todorov.evidence_note: Own1997P21 directly qualifies his appreciation of ideal types and describes the disputed stance as Weber’s Nietzscheanism. This is Todorov’s interpretation, not independent verification that it exhausts Weber. Strauss/Aron debate contextual mediation retained; originals unread and no invented direct exchange.

tzvetan_todorov.relationship: Todorov questions the coherence between Derrida’s democratic commitments and deconstruction’s treatment of values, while acknowledging the theory’s internal sophistication.
tzvetan_todorov.evidence_note: Own1997P25 explicitly locates his objection between public ethical commitments and professional philosophy, not an internal logical refutation. Blanchot’s anti-value statement supplies a separate example, not a quote assigned to Derrida. P27 retains friendship/intellectual admiration but says Derrida did not answer his philosophical interests. Spanish rendering; underlying Derrida/Blanchot texts unread.

tzvetan_todorov.relationship: Todorov adapts Arendt’s banality-of-evil argument when explaining his own emphasis on ordinary acts of good rather than exceptional heroism.
tzvetan_todorov.evidence_note: Own 1997 P37 explicitly calls his banality of good similar and contrary to Arendt’s argument yet grounded in the same reasons; conceptual adaptation, not simple disagreement or denial of evil. P21 separately names Arendt among a plural philosophical education without implying full agreement. Eichmann book and full Facing Extreme originals unread; interviewer’s framing distinguished.

tzvetan_todorov.relationship: Todorov challenges Horkheimer and Adorno’s pessimistic Enlightenment narrative for treating a real but avoidable historical development as if it had to culminate in totalitarianism.
tzvetan_todorov.evidence_note: Actual own answer in opening 2016 interview, published 2020, names both coauthors; Horkheimer lacks endpoint but shared responsibility retained. Todorov concedes shadows and potential threats of Enlightenment, so this is not denial of its destructive uses. Only displayed opening read; original Dialectic and rest of interview unread. Precise question supplied instead of fabricated page.

tzvetan_todorov.relationship: Leichter reports Ricœur’s approving use of Todorov’s warning that claims to victim status can generate demands on others, within Ricœur’s distinction between justice for other victims and self-victimization.
tzvetan_todorov.evidence_note: Explicitly named 2012 scholarly mediation 124–125/nn68–69 directs to English Memory, History, Forgetting 86. This scoped quotation/use is not broad agreement on every duty-of-memory issue, and does not make Leichter an original formative source.

tzvetan_todorov.relationship: Todorov describes introducing Russian Formalist approaches into French literary debate through his 1965 translated anthology and subsequent editorial work with Jakobson.
tzvetan_todorov.evidence_note: Own1997P13–15 details translation/selection, Genette’s editorial introduction, Sollers/Pleynet’s publication role and Jakobson’s advice/preface;2001 interviewsample6–7 describes continued editing/translation assistance. tzvetan_todorov.evidence_note: Own translated retrospective sample8–9 explicitly states this intellectual and communicative objection. named_group_routes.evidence_note: The user kept them apart (2026-10-12): the framework is "a different project closer to history of capitalism". Pâquet links the framework to studies of "liberal social regulation", and Valverde places moral reform at the centre of English Canada's race, class and gender organization. named_group_routes.relationship: Foucauldian analysis contributes to the concept of moral regulation and its governmentality reformulation
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Ruonavaara's abstract describes Corrigan and Sayer's framework as fusing Durkheimian and Foucauldian analysis with basic Marxist theory; Dean's abstract argues that problems in Corrigan's account are better formulated through Foucault's problematic of governmentality. Drawn as a contribution, the atlas's usual kind for Foucault's outgoing edges. Valverde's own acknowledgement (checked 2026-10-14 for revision 1.136, in Google Books search-within snippets of the 2008 reissue, 1991 pagination): 'Following but modifying Foucault's approach, I take the term "discourses" to refer not to language as separate from the real world but rather to organized sets of signifying practices' (preface, p. x) and 'as Foucault and his followers have pointed out, the state has no monopoly on moral regulation' (p. 165; also quoted by Dehli 1992, p. 317). Wright (Acadiensis, 1995, p. 123, read) reads her as modifying 'Foucault's archaeology' with 'an important commitment to social agency'. Strange and Loo (1997, p. 5, snippet): 'Theorists influenced by philosopher Michel Foucault have urged scholars to abandon the social-control model for a more flexible concept of regulation'. Not a claim about every Canadian study in the roster.

named_group_routes.relationship: Protestant reformers as regulators and as religious actors
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Valverde studies the moral fervour of Protestant social reformers (publisher description); the religion-and-reform entry studies the same churches and social gospel as religious history (Christie and Gauvreau 1996, title-level). The two fields read the reformers differently. In period, Loo (Labour/Le Travail 30, 1992, p. 278, read) asked Valverde's book to 'address Christianity and certainly Protestantism more fully, even if only to dismiss its importance', and Christie and Gauvreau (1996, p. xiii, Google Books snippet) said she and Doug Owram used 'a caricature of the antiquated and esoteric Victorian theologue to excise the churches'. Those objections concern one book and are recorded on the edge from the mariana_valverde entry (revision 1.136); this field-level edge stays a comparison. Valverde places moral reform at the centre of English Canada's race, class and gender order; Cook's Regenerators covers the same reformers' religious thought. Comparison only.

named_group_routes.relationship: Moral reform, racial purity and law
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Valverde's reformers linked sexual health to racial purity (publisher description); Backhouse's Colour-Coded traces racism through law (title-level). PhD context: 72 of 149 2009–2026 PhDs engaging Moral regulation also engage Immigration, ethnicity & race in Canada (48%; lift 3.99), counted after removing shared anchors (Backhouse). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.

named_group_routes.relationship: Relations and encounter versus a structure of dispossession
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The same archives and subjects (reserves, schools, policy) are read as relations and encounter here and as a continuing settler structure in the Settler colonialism entry. Greer argues the settler mode dominates some periods and regions and fades in others; commercial penetration, the fur-trade mode, is another. Most native–newcomer works predate the settler framework and do not adopt it. PhD context: among 2009–2026 PhDs engaging this roster (two or more people cited), the share also citing Wolfe’s or Veracini’s settler-colonial works rises from 1 of 66 (2009–14) to 14 of 88 (2015–19) and 26 of 65 (2020–26), while engagement with the roster holds steady (16.1% → 16.0% of all PhDs). Bibliographies record consultation, not adoption.

named_group_routes.relationship: Indigenous historical authority and settler-colonial analysis
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Konishi surveys Indigenous scholars who advocate, interrogate and challenge settler colonial studies (abstract). Revision of 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md P.6, p4B_rel_12) adds the read words on both sides. Kauanui 2016 (read in full): 'Settler Colonial Studies does not, should not, and cannot replace Indigenous Studies'; Wolfe 'insisted … that Native scholars did' create the field; indigeneity 'a category of analysis that is distinct from race, ethnicity, and nationality'. Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel 2014, pp. 9–11 (read): the field 'can displace, overshadow, or even mask over Indigenous studies'; 'when settlers take up these questions, it's suddenly considered a legitimate field of study'. Goeman 2016 (read in full): Wolfe's work 'became a place to engage Indigenous studies concerns in relation to settler colonial studies that at times leaves out Indigenous epistemologies and ontologies'. Veracini 2013 (author manuscript, read): 'indigenous studies, and especially history became crucial disciplinary sites in the development of "settler colonialism" as a conceptual category'. Comparison only: Indigenous history is not a subset of the paradigm, and the paradigm did not originate there. The earlier note's Canadian PhD counts are moved to the entry's scope_note.

named_group_routes.relationship: Land, labour and elementary structures of race
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Wolfe's AHR forum essay and later book compare regimes of race through land and labour. Title level only: the weakest proposal, optional.

named_group_routes.relationship: Scott's theory of gender is weighed in Canadian debates over discourse, experience and gender history
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Valverde's 1990 review essay in Labour/Le Travail, read in full, treats Scott's Gender and the Politics of History (with Riley) as a key work in 'the controversy about discourse theory'. She notes that poststructuralism had a 'bad reputation … among socialists and feminists (in English Canada, at least)' and that 'in Canada' the debate was posed as 'a yes-or-no question'. She concludes that Scott 'deserves to be carefully read even by those who find some of its more polemical claims hard to swallow'. Pierson's 1991 essay on Canadian women's history opens on the turn to deconstruction, with Scott's theorising of gender as its most acclaimed example (opening read). Reference lists show Scott cited by Linda Kealey (1992), Pierson (1992) and Parr's 1995 CHR essay on gender history (OpenAlex metadata; texts unread). Limits: the evidence shows engagement and debate, not adoption. Valverde is sympathetic but critical. Palmer's Descent into Discourse (1990) is a Canadian critique of the linguistic turn, but its treatment of Scott was not checked here. The 1995–96 Left History exchange is title-level and is not evidence that names Scott. PhD context: 64 of 120 Canadian History PhDs citing Scott engage this field (53%, lift 2.12); 39 engage childhood and youth (lift 3.21), and 49 working-class history (lift 1.87).

named_group_routes.relationship: Settler colonialism as 'a structure not an event': settler colonizers 'come to stay'; the form 'destroys to replace', is 'inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal', has territory as its 'irreducible element' and persists after the frontier as 'structural genocide' (1994–2006)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Revision of 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md P.6, p4B_rel_01): the 2006 essay, read in full in the Internet Archive capture of the journal's free-to-read page (screq_wolfe_2006 addendum), joins the 1999 introduction (pp. 1–2, read earlier: settler colonies 'were (are) premised on the elimination of native societies'; 'invasion is a structure not an event'; contents and catalogue checked). Wolfe 2006, in his words: 'Settler colonialism is inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal' (p. 387, pages per Kauanui 2016); 'Territoriality is settler colonialism's specific, irreducible element'; 'settler colonizers come to stay: invasion is a structure not an event' (p. 388; his note 7 refers the formula to the 1999 book, p. 2, and to 'Nation and MiscegeNation', 1994, p. 96); 'Settler colonialism destroys to replace'; 'elimination refers to more than the summary liquidation of Indigenous people, though it includes that' (p. 390); 'settler colonialism is relatively impervious to regime change'; 'structural genocide' (p. 403). A contribution, not a founding: earlier settler-society studies (1983, 1995) and earlier usage (Veracini 2013; Kauanui 2016, note 7: Sayegh 1965, Rodinson 1973) precede it, and Kauanui records that Wolfe 'insisted … that he did not create the field of settler colonial studies—that Native scholars did'. The earlier note's Canadian PhD counts are moved to the entry's scope_note (user rule, 2026-10-23); bibliographies record consultation, not influence.

named_group_routes.relationship: A history of Victorian and Australian anthropology in its settler-colonial setting
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period evidence (1999). The contents page lists chapters on mother-right ('Sex and Property in Victorian Anthropology'), totemism ('Victorian Anthropology's Eternal Dichotomy') and E. B. Tylor ('Survival in a Paradigm Shift: E.B. Tylor and the Problem of the Text'), alongside virgin birth in anthropology and in Australian settler discourse. Catalogue subjects: Anthropology -- Australia -- History; Racism in anthropology -- Australia. Introduction p. 1 read: the book is 'a history not so much of anthropology itself as of its ideological entanglements'. The chapters' stance toward these anthropologists is not read here. If the introduction confirms a critical argument, a critique edge to anthropology/evolution may be the better reading. A historian's account of the discipline, not anthropological fieldwork. Addendum 2026-10-23 (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md P.6, p4B_rel_02): Veracini's obituary (read in full) reports that the 1999 book 'was ostensibly a history of Australian anthropology', that 'settler colonialism' was 'only added at the very end and at the request of the publisher', and that 'to explain the evolution of anthropology Patrick defined settler colonialism as distinct from colonialism'; Goeman (read in full) records Audra Simpson's memory of him as a historian 'of anthropology itself, and its relationship to politics'. The chapters remain unread, so the critique/contribution question stays open.

named_group_routes.relationship: Gender and class as simultaneous hierarchies, and gender history as a practice in Canadian women's history (1985–96)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period, her own words (Atlantis, 1985, read in full): women and children are not tied together as subjects by nature; 'What distinguishes feminine and preschooler from masculine and prime of life is not naturalness versus artificiality but proximity to power' (p. 39). She criticises the mid-1970s Canadian literature on reform for characterising 1880–1920 as 'an era of "maternal feminism"', seeing women's public actions 'definitionally as an extension of the private' (p. 41), and asks historians to 'stop shying away from the word "patriarchy"' and to 'allow as a possibility that gender/sex hierarchies and class hierarchies function simultaneously, each according to its own logic, often in conflict' (p. 44). She presents this as a change 'a good many others have already begun to suggest' (p. 39). The Gender of Breadwinners (1990), unread here, as reviewers quote it: Guildford (Atlantis, 1991, p. 140) says she rejects 'an ahistorical hierarchy of oppressions' (p. 8) and argues 'that class and gender are made and experienced simultaneously'; Bertaux (JEH, 1992, p. 241) quotes p. 9 on 'these galloping pairs—class/gender, male/female, market/nonmarket, public/private' whose meanings 'are multiple and mutable'. Reception in the Left History exchange (all read in full): Sangster calls the book 'One of the path breaking books on gender history' (1995, p. 120); Iacovetta and Kealey call her 'recognized as a leading practitioner of gender history' (1996, p. 222) and 'a major figure in the field', quoting her 1995 CHR essay (pp. 362–63) that 'gender history made masculinity and femininity commensurably problematical historically, while insisting that neither could be well understood without companion inquiries into the other hierarchies with which they were mutually intertwined' (p. 228); Dubinsky and Marks cite her for refraining 'from imposing one category - be it class or gender - on historical actors' (1996, p. 211). Criticism: Sangster (1996, p. 240 n. 2) characterises Parr's essay (its reprint in Gender and History in Canada, 1996, p. 11, unread here) as placing critics 'feminist and anti-feminist alike, in the same oppositional group' (Sangster's wording, not a quotation from Parr), notes that she had been reproached for not offering 'more criticism of historians such as Mariana Valverde and Joy Parr' (p. 240 n. 3), and, quoting Parr's line that the move to gender 'began from the post-structuralist premise that identities were made in relationships' (reprint p. 14), questions 'the prevailing assumption that gender history as the field, post-structuralism as the method, equals a superior, more broad-minded history' (pp. 244, 246). The 1995 essay itself is unread: its words here are quoted by Iacovetta and Kealey and by Sangster. Not a founding: the field's gender debate also runs through Pierson (1991) and Scott (edge_891). Later reading, labelled: a 2026 CHR 'great books' forum (abstract only) calls the book 'a path-breaking study that challenged established dichotomies in social theory'.

named_group_routes.relationship: Moral regulation as the formation of ethical subjectivity, carried out by philanthropies, churches and professions as well as the state: social purity in English Canada, 1885–1925 (1991–92; the 1988 article with Weir is listed but unread)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements. 'Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State', Labour/Le Travail 30 (1992), pp. 213–222, read in full: 'I have argued elsewhere that the discourse of moral reform needs to be analyzed seriously, not merely dismissed as a cover for class interests', though 'moral discourse does as a matter of contingent fact legitimize certain class, gender, and racial interests' (p. 216); she credits Corrigan and Sayer's The Great Arch with pioneering 'the liberal state's role in constituting subjectivities' (p. 217). The Age of Light, Soap, and Water (1991) is known here through in-period reviewers' quotations and through Google Books search-within snippets of the 2008 University of Toronto Press reissue (volume ghqEyXf5950C; partial preview, page images not viewable here because the viewing limit was reached), which keep the 1991 pagination: reformers sought 'to reshape the ethical subjectivity of both immigrants and native-born Canadians' (p. 17; quoted by Dehli 1992, p. 316); purity work 'was not simply a question of banning obscene books or suppressing prostitution but was rather a campaign to educate the next generation' (p. 17; quoted by McCormick 1992, p. 124); the reform movements 'helped to shape the bourgeoisie, which led the movements, as well as the working class' (p. 15; Dehli, p. 318); 'Moral regulation is very closely linked to state formation, as the British school of historical sociology has argued; but as Foucault and his followers have pointed out, the state has no monopoly on moral regulation' (p. 165; snippet, the last clause also quoted by Dehli, p. 317); '[m]oral regulation is an important aspect of ruling, helping to constitute class, gender, sexual, and race relations' (p. 166, as quoted by Wright 1995, p. 124). Her notes, seen only as snippets, place the concept: in The Great Arch 'the role of the state in moral regulation is highlighted, and their theorization has been influential here; but the agencies of regulation internal to civil society are obscured' (n. 34, p. 171); Corrigan and Sayer 'do not differentiate between moral and other modes of social regulation; by contrast, I restrict the term to mean the formation of ethical subjectivity' (p. 173). Note 33 (p. 171) cites the 1988 article with Lorna Weir, which is unread here. In-period reception by historians. Tina Loo (Labour/Le Travail 30, 1992, pp. 277–279, read) calls the book 'a provocative and valuable contribution to the history of social reform and, more significantly, because of its self-conscious use of theory, to the writing of Canadian history' (p. 279). Donald Wright (Acadiensis, 1995, pp. 122–126 read) calls it a 'much talked about treatise' by 'a sociologist' (p. 122) and its concept of 'slippages' among class, gender, sexuality and race her 'most original' contribution (p. 124). Carolyn Strange and Tina Loo's Making Good: Law and Moral Regulation in Canada (1997; Google Books snippets, pp. 5, 63) write that 'Theorists influenced by philosopher Michel Foucault have urged scholars to abandon the social-control model for a more flexible concept of regulation' (p. 5) and cite 'Mariana Valverde and others' on prostitution as 'the social evil' (p. 63). Mary Louise Adams's 'In Sickness and in Health: State Formation, Moral Regulation, and Early VD Initiatives in Ontario' (1994) is cited at title level only. In-period criticism. Loo finds the second argument, on philanthropy and the state, 'more asserted than proved' (p. 279). Kari Dehli (Historical Studies in Education, 1992, pp. 315–319, read) would draw 'not quite so sharply drawn' conclusions about state and civil society and finds that she moves 'quickly from analysis of discursive strategies ... to drawing conclusions about people's motives and intentions' (pp. 318–319). Wright judges her claim that audiences 'knew precisely what was meant' 'untenable' and finds 'the impoverished immigrant and the "fallen woman" ... conspicuously silent', so that 'the silence of the consumer amidst the din of the producer gives the impression of top-down social control, precisely what Valverde sought to avoid' (pp. 125–126). Chris McCormick (Atlantis, 1992, pp. 123–125, read) asks how her interpretations are made and judges that a 'thorough' reading of context is 'optimistic' (p. 123), while agreeing that 'Regulation is a better word than control' (p. 124). Sociologists reformulated the concept: Alan Hunt's 1997 abstract (read) treats moral regulation not as 'a specific moral arena' but as 'a component of all fields of social relations', a wider definition than hers; in Governing Morals (1999; snippets) he writes 'I do not take issue with Valverde's invocation of ethical subjectivity, but I emphasise the mundane features of self-governing' (p. 155). Dean (1994) and Ruonavaara (1997) are cited through their abstracts as on the moral_regulation node. A contribution, not a founding: Corrigan (1981) and Corrigan and Sayer (1985) precede her, and she credits them. Diseases of the Will (1998), on alcohol and the governance of the will, is title-level here (snippets only) and does not support this edge.
