named_group_routes.relationship: Protestant reformers read as moral regulators rather than as religious actors, and the church historians' objection that this excised the churches from progressive thought (1991–96)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her object overlaps the field's. The book studies Methodist and Presbyterian church organizations, the Salvation Army, the WCTU, the YWCA and the National Council of Women (Dehli 1992, p. 316, read), with familiar reformers such as Chown, Shearer and Woodsworth (Loo 1992, p. 277, read). Her reading is regulatory: purity work 'was rather a campaign to educate the next generation' (p. 17, quoted by McCormick 1992, p. 124), and the discourse of moral reform 'needs to be analyzed seriously, not merely dismissed as a cover for class interests' ('Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State', 1992, p. 216, read). In-period objections from historians of religion and reform. Loo (Labour/Le Travail 30, 1992, p. 278, read) finds that 'religion and sectarian differences' get 'rather short shrift', suggests Richard Allen's typology of radical, progressive and conservative reformers, and holds that 'any discussion of the discourse of moral reform in Canada needs to address Christianity and certainly Protestantism more fully, even if only to dismiss its importance'. Nancy Christie and Michael Gauvreau, A Full-Orbed Christianity (1996), known here only through Google Books search-within snippets: 'historians such as Doug Owram and Mariana Valverde have adhered to a caricature of the antiquated and esoteric Victorian theologue to excise the churches from "progressive" currents of modern thought and social action' (p. xiii); 'Valverde has argued that in early twentieth-century Canada issues such as social purity and immigration were controlled by a hegemonic exercise of power by the state and middle-class organizations' (p. 187), and her analysis 'wrongly posits the view that given the hegemonic influence of the state, there was only one option regarding immigration policy – that of racism and the annihilation of immigrant culture', against which they set 'three divergent strands of opinion on the immigration question' among Protestant clergy (p. 188; n. 95, p. 328, cites her pp. 15, 112, 123–8). Their p. 187 summary attributes to her a state-centred hegemony that her own p. 165 qualifies ('the state has no monopoly on moral regulation'); the disagreement is recorded, not adjudicated. A comparison, as her roster row and edge_861 (moral_regulation – cdn_religion_reform) have it: the criticism runs from the church historians to her, and she did not answer it in a text read here. The dispute is person-level, which is why it is drawn from her entry; edge_861 stays the field-level comparison.

named_group_routes.relationship: Liberalism read as a system of moral regulation and the liberal state as a constitutor of subjectivities (1991–92), beside the liberal order framework's later history of property, the individual and rule
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own in-period statements, before McKay's prospectus (2000). 'Pauperism, Moral Character, and the Liberal State', Labour/Le Travail 30 (1992), pp. 213–222, read in full, endorses Mitchell Dean's argument 'that classical English liberalism was not a negation of state regulation but rather a particular system of economic, social, and moral regulation', so that 'a history of pauperism is also a genealogy of liberalism' (p. 217). She reviews Jean-Marie Fecteau's Un nouvel ordre des choses (1989) as 'a landmark work' whose 'theoretical sophistication' crosses 'the traditional historiographical boundaries separating coercion from benevolence and the state as a whole from charity' (pp. 221–222), but faults its 'moyens de contrôle' as 'a rather functionalist formulation', a 'model of negative class power', and adds that 'These moral codes are not intrinsic to the logic of capital, since capitalism works quite efficiently in different cultural systems' (p. 222). Note 10 (p. 220) cites Fecteau's essay in Greer and Radforth's Colonial Leviathan (1992), and the essay thanks Allan Greer for comments on a draft (p. 222). In the 1991 book (Google Books search-within snippets of the 2008 reissue, 1991 pagination) note 35 (p. 171) cites Bruce Curtis's 'Preconditions of the Canadian State', and she writes that moral regulation 'might be an important social process, which is intertwined with but is not an effect of either the economic or the political' (p. 165) and that 'one has to be sceptical of any claims that envision a clear separation between moral and economic regulation' (p. 166). Reviewers read the book's state argument in the same terms: private philanthropy 'allowed liberal democratic states to adhere to their policy of non-interference in the private sphere' (Loo 1992, p. 278, her paraphrase). Comparison only. The user decided (2026-10-12) that the liberal order framework is 'a different project closer to history of capitalism'; Fecteau and Curtis are shared ground (state formation), not membership. No in-period text by the framework's authors discussing her was read here (McKay's 2000 prospectus is paywalled and unread). edge_848 (liberal_order_framework – moral_regulation) is the field-level comparison. This edge is an editorial comparison of her 1992 argument with the later framework (McKay, 2000); she did not distinguish herself from a framework not yet formulated.

named_group_routes.relationship: Scott's poststructuralist programme criticised by a sympathetic reader, who suggested that it may exaggerate what Foucault and Derrida can do for historians, for passing over discourse analysis's bias towards 'the sociology of domination', and (1995) for setting theory against working-class history
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own in-period words (1990 essay read in full; 1995 essay, pp. 329–332 read). 'Poststructuralist Gender Historians: Are We Those Names?', Labour/Le Travail 25 (1990), pp. 227–236, reviews Scott's Gender and the Politics of History with Denise Riley's 'Am I That Name?'. She grants that Scott's approach 'has much to commend it' but finds her four elements of gender 'somewhat arbitrary' and asks whether the definition 'finally succeeds in transcending the idealism/materialism dichotomy' (p. 230). Scott's case studies show limitations 'symptomatic of the general limitations of discourse analysis as it has been used by social historians (myself included!)' (p. 231): there is 'an inherent bias in discourse analysis in favour of what some call "the sociology of domination." This problem, not discussed by Scott, does not discredit or make redundant discourse analysis' (p. 232). Scott's 'rather polemical book tends to sing the praises of discourse analysis without mentioning many of its problems', with a 'grandiose claim made by Scott on Foucault's behalf' (p. 232), and 'It may be that she exaggerates the contribution Foucault and Derrida can make to historical work' (p. 233). She ends that 'Scott's work deserves to be carefully read even by those who find some of its more polemical claims hard to swallow' (p. 233). 'Deconstructive Marxism', Labour/Le Travail 36 (1995), pp. 329–340 (pp. 329–332 read), sharpens the judgment: Scott 'made an influential attempt to extend the reach of deconstruction within historical writing to the certainties of class. Her argument was limited in many ways' (pp. 331–332); 'Scott probably used her new-found theories to justify a break with Marxism that she, like so many other former leftists on both sides of the Atlantic, wanted to make anyway', and 'the book undoubtedly made an important contribution to the feminist analysis of both politics and history: but it did so, or at least gave the appearance of doing so, at the expense of working-class history' (p. 332). She criticises the other side too: 'for many labour historians, any hint of theoretical sophistication became prima faciae evidence of political backsliding' (p. 332), and her note names Bryan Palmer's Descent into Discourse as 'the by now standard Marxist critique of Scott' (p. 332, n. 5). edge_891 (joan_wallach_scott → cdn_women_gender) already cites the 1990 essay as evidence of Canadian engagement with Scott; this edge records her own criticism of Scott's position, which edge_891 does not carry. A critique within broad sympathy, not a rejection: the qualifications above are part of the claim.

named_group_routes.relationship: Foucault criticised for discounting individual authors (1978) and for ignoring empire and dissolving the individual in a 'microphysics of power' that it is 'hopeless to resist' (1993)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Said's own in-period statements. Orientalism (1978): 'Foucault believes that in general the individual text or author counts for very little; empirically, in the case of Orientalism (and perhaps nowhere else) I find this not to be so' (p. 23), while declaring himself 'greatly indebted' to Foucault (p. 23). Culture and Imperialism (Knopf, 1993): of Foucault and Raymond Williams, 'In the main I am in considerable sympathy with the genealogical discoveries of these two formidable scholars, and greatly indebted to them. Yet for both the imperial experience is quite irrelevant, a theoretical oversight that is the norm in Western cultural and scientific disciplines' (p. 41). Comparing Foucault and Fanon: 'Foucault's work moves further and further away from serious consideration of social wholes, focussing instead upon the individual as dissolved in an ineluctably advancing "microphysics of power" that it is hopeless to resist'; 'ignoring the imperial context of his own theories, Foucault seems actually to represent an irresistible colonizing movement that paradoxically fortifies the prestige of both the lonely individual scholar and the system that contains him'; Foucault 'swerves away from politics entirely' (p. 278). His note 198 refers the reader to 'my critique in "Foucault and the Imagination of Power"' (in David Hoy, ed., Foucault: A Critical Reader, 1986, pp. 149–155); that essay, and 'Traveling Theory' (1983), were not read. On p. 26 he also describes Foucault's turn to 'the local micro-physics of power that surround the individual'. Foucault's position is given only as Said presents it; no reply by Foucault was looked for. The critique is from a writer who kept using Foucault (edge 2); it is a disagreement within an acknowledged debt. edge_386 (post → foucault, Spivak and Stoler) records other postcolonial critics' engagements and stays.

named_group_routes.relationship: Culture and Imperialism's account of resistance culture: anticolonial histories such as James's The Black Jacobins and Antonius's The Arab Awakening read as a 'voyage in' to metropolitan culture, alongside post-independence critiques by Guha and Alatas (1993)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own in-period text. Culture and Imperialism (Knopf, 1993), chapter 3, 'Resistance and Opposition'. He distinguishes liberal anti-colonialism, which did 'not dispute the fundamental superiority of Western man', from anti-imperialism, and argues 'there was no overall condemnation of imperialism until—and this is my point—after native uprisings were too far gone to be ignored or defeated' (pp. 240–241). Anti-imperialist work by writers from the peripheries in the metropolis is 'usually an extension into the metropolis of large-scale mass movements'; 'There is thus an overlap and interdependence that cannot theoretically be described as only the reactive assertion of a separate colonial or native identity'; 'The voyage in, then, constitutes an especially interesting variety of hybrid cultural work' (p. 244). He reads 'C.L.R. James's The Black Jacobins, published in 1938, and, appearing at almost the same time, George Antonius's The Arab Awakening' as works 'intended as serious works of scholarship and advocacy addressed from within a national movement for independence to a general audience', set against Ranajit Guha's A Rule of Property for Bengal (1963) and S. H. Alatas's The Myth of the Lazy Native (1977), which are 'post-colonial and specialist' (p. 245); 'history for Guha is critique, not the dutiful replication of colonialist objects, ideologies, and arguments' (p. 251). He also treats Fanon as one who 'programmatically seeks to treat colonial and metropolitan societies together' (p. 278). The introduction frames the chapter: 'What I left out of Orientalism was that response to Western dominance which culminated in the great movement of decolonization' (p. xii). Read: pp. xii, 240–245, 251, 278; the rest of the chapter (including the Fanon and Cabral sections) was not read closely. No in-period review assessing this chapter for historians was read. A contribution to how anticolonial histories are read and placed, not a claim that he wrote anticolonial history in their sense; The Question of Palestine (1979) is mentioned in the node, not used for this edge.
