named_group_routes.relationship: Colonial Leviathan (1992, edited with Ian Radforth): mid-nineteenth-century state formation in the Canadas, written before the framework was named, and later faulted by Greer himself for neglecting Indigenous peoples (2019)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Colonial Leviathan is unread (lending-only copy; the Érudit, Left History and Histoire sociale reviews returned bot checks). In-period reading: Palmer (Labour/Le Travail 31, 1993, read in full) says the volume and Curtis's book 'are searching for the state in pre-Confederation Canada' (p. 365) and finds that 'the collection lacks coherence', while its 'single most important contribution ... also developed by Curtis, is the notion that the coming of ‘responsible government’ actually entailed the subversion of the reform strategy of the 1830s' (p. 366); he names Greer's chapter on the birth of the police (p. 366). Valverde's 1992 essay cites Fecteau's chapter in the volume (edge_966). Greer's own later judgment (2019, read): 'The time may be right, then, for a renewed history of the Confederation era, one that unites the history of state formation with that of settler colonialism' (p. 73), with n. 41: 'A prime example of this problem would be Colonial Leviathan; devoted to questions of state formation, it neglected everything to do with Indigenous peoples and processes of elimination' (p. 84). Comparison only: the volume predates McKay's prospectus (2000), and no checked text by McKay or his commentators names it; Pâquet (2009) links the framework to studies of state formation in general. The atlas's state_formation_roots strand places it there editorially.

named_group_routes.relationship: Settler colonialism historicised as one mode of colonial invasion among several, beside imperial/commercial penetration and extractivism, dominant in some periods and regions of northern North America and not others: a sympathetic critique that keeps Wolfe's 'structure, not an event' (2018–19)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own words, all after 2000 and dated. 'Settler Colonialism and Beyond' (Journal of the CHA 30, 2019, read in full; a CHA keynote): settler colonial theory 'does indeed have much to offer historians', but over 500 years of invasion 'the settler variety stands out as a dominant force in some periods and regions, but it fades to insignificance in others' (p. 62); 'The late Patrick Wolfe, still the most important theorist of settler colonialism' (p. 62); the danger of 'temporal flattening' 'when settler colonialism is casually invoked in ways that suggest a transhistorical, always-already quality' (p. 63); 'Let me assure you that I am not here to trash or dismiss settler-colonial theory' and, with Wolfe, settler colonialism is 'a structure, not an event'; 'However, that doesn't mean we need to find settler colonialism everywhere and all the time' (p. 63); 'Imperial/Commercial Penetration' and 'Extractivism' are 'coexisting and overlapping versions of colonialism' (p. 64); early settlements 'hardly functioned as instruments of elimination and replacement except in quite limited, localized ways' (p. 64); 'To those who insist that Canada is, was, and always has been a settler-colonial phenomenon, I offer qualified support' (p. 73); 'settlers as such are no longer the main threat, for the invasion has adopted a different guise' (p. 74); and 'Settler colonialism stands out also as a fundamental force behind the creation of a territorial nation-state' (p. 79). Property and Dispossession (2018), introduction read on Cambridge Core (no page markers): 'Some scholars speak of an “eliminationist” logic driving settler colonialism ... toward the utter destruction of natives who stand in its way', but 'such “ethnic cleansing” is not the whole story' (n. 25 cites Wolfe 2006). The target is the field, not patrick_wolfe: Greer accepts Wolfe's structure thesis and objects to how the term is commonly used, citing Woolford and Benvenuto's warning that it risks becoming 'a reductive shorthand' (p. 63). The William and Mary Quarterly essay (2019) is unread beyond its recorded opening.

named_group_routes.relationship: British Columbia's reserve system explained as geographical dispossession: a capacity resting on state-backed force, a momentum from capital and settlers, a legitimation in a discourse of civilization and savagery, and a management by 'disciplinary technologies' of maps, numbers, law and the land system (1997–2004); written in a settler society's terms ('successful settler colonialism', 2003), with no derivation from Wolfe's theory established by the texts checked, and faulted by reviewers for few Native voices
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own words. 'Revisiting the Native Land Question', BC Studies 138/139 (2003), pp. 137–151, his précis of Making Native Space, read in full: the reserves comprised 'slightly more than one-third of 1 per cent of provincial land' (p. 137); 'The capacity to dispossess rested on raw firepower authorized, usually, by the administrative superstructure of the state. … The momentum to dispossess came from capital seeking profits and from settlers seeking livelihoods' (p. 137); 'The legitimation of dispossession lay with a cultural discourse that located civilization and savagery … the implementation of dispossession rested with a set of disciplinary technologies among which maps, numbers, and, especially, the common law were essential' (p. 138); 'two very different stories underlie British Columbia. One is about progress and development … It rests, however, on the other basic story about this place, which is about dispossession, loss, marginalization, and the struggle for survival' (p. 140); 'Given the values and benefits associated with successful settler colonialism, many British Columbians will find this an exceedingly difficult commitment' (p. 144, of a politics of difference). The 2004 abstract (publisher's abstract via OpenAlex; article unread) states the same four conclusions: 'the initial ability to dispossess rested primarily on physical power and the supporting infrastructure of the state; the momentum to dispossess derived from the interest of capital in profit and of settlers in forging new livelihoods; the legitimation of and moral justification for dispossession lay in a cultural discourse that located civilization and savagery …; and the management of dispossession rested with a set of disciplinary technologies of which maps, numbers, law, and the geography of resettlement itself were the most important.' In-period reception. Tina Loo, review of The Resettlement of British Columbia, BC Studies 117 (1998), pp. 64–67, read in full: Harris 'locates the non-Native settlement of British Columbia explicitly in the context of the expansion of European imperial and commercial power' and sees colonization as 'the displacement of Indigenous peoples and the remaking of space that was formerly theirs into an immigrant society' (p. 64); but 'there are very few "Native voices" in it - something Harris himself admits', and Native peoples, 'despite a few examples to the contrary, emerge as victims' (p. 66); in the later chapters 'the connections to colonization … increasingly fade away' and class is not discussed (pp. 66–67); still 'a provocative and important book' (p. 67). Daniel Clayton, BC Studies 138/139 (2003), pp. 5–11, read in full: 'Harris's most political work to date and arguably the most significant contribution to our understanding of colonialism in the province since Robin Fisher's Contact and Conflict (1977)' (p. 6). Jo-Anne Fiske, commentary in the 2003 forum (pp. 151–155, read): he 'says little … of how a change in mindset and a marshalling of political will might be achieved', and what he says of the symbolic 'is unsettling in its apparent simplicity' (p. 152); the powers he describes 'did not and cannot exist outside of the symbolic realm' (p. 152). Harris replied: 'I doubt that Jo-Anne Fiske and I have any real disagreement' (p. 161). Val Napoleon (2004): see pe139_harris_rel_07. No derivation from Wolfe is established by the texts checked: they cite Merivale, Kymlicka and Macklem, not Wolfe, and the books are unread; the settler_colonialism roster already says Harris wrote 'earlier or beside' the paradigm. Later reading, labelled: Perry (BC Studies 190, 2016, p. 112) says her 2001 book read British Columbia 'within a comparative framework of settler colonialism, echoing an assumption that undergirds Cole Harris's 1997 and 2002 books'. A Bounded Land (2020), with its 'Postscript: The Boundaries of Settler Colonialism', is cited at title level only.

named_group_routes.relationship: Colonial-discourse studies criticised for an emphasis on culture that 'tends to obscure other forms of colonial power'; he proposed explaining 'colonialism's basic geographical dispossessions of the colonized' instead, while allowing that 'several theoretical perspectives yield crucial insights' (2004)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own words. Abstract of 'How Did Colonialism Dispossess? Comments from an Edge of Empire', Annals of the Association of American Geographers 94:1 (2004), pp. 165–182 (publisher's abstract, read via OpenAlex; article body closed and unread): 'The emphasis on culture in studies of colonialism tends to obscure other forms of colonial power while making it impossible to contextualize the cultural argument and assess its salience. Rather than focusing on texts, systems of signification, and procedures of knowledge generation, as the colonial discourse literature is wont to do, a fuller understanding of colonial powers is achieved by explaining colonialism's basic geographical dispossessions of the colonized. In so doing, the issue of power is not prejudged'; it ends 'Although no one body of theory explains colonial power, several theoretical perspectives yield crucial insights.' The 2003 précis (BC Studies, pp. 137–138, read) gives culture one of four roles, the legitimation of dispossession. Qualifications: he uses the literature he criticises. In 1997–98 (p. 59 n. 39, read) he cites Said's Orientalism as 'The original and most influential discussion' of the European categories of civilized and savage; Napoleon (2004, p. 114, read) finds Making Native Space 'Informed by Frantz Fanon, Edward Said, Michel Foucault, and E.P. Thompson'. Clayton's reading, labelled as his (2003, read): Harris is 'neither a close student of the imperial imagination nor a slavish follower of the powerful postcolonial theories' (p. 8, Clayton's paraphrase); his findings fuel 'his suspicion of an international postcolonial literature that, in his view, tends to overplay the hands of culture and discourse relative to other forms of power' (pp. 8–9, citing the 2004 essay as forthcoming); yet he 'favours (again however unwittingly) a certain postcolonial narrative' (p. 9) and 'has absorbed a body of ideas about the ascriptive power of colonial discourse … that were initially advanced by Said' (p. 10). No reply from a postcolonial critic was checked.
named_group_routes.map_label: Harris: culture overweighted in colonial-discourse studies, 2003–04

named_group_routes.relationship: Foucault's sovereign and disciplinary power as Harris's terms for the fur traders' 'politics of fear' and for the colonial land system and its 'disciplinary technologies' (1997–2004), used selectively
named_group_routes.evidence_note: His own words. 1997–98 (BC Studies 115/116, p. 58, read): the traders' retaliations 'in public theatres of power' were 'what Michel Foucault called sovereign power, a sporadic, local, and highly visible seizure of property or life', quoting Discipline and Punish (n. 37); he adds that 'In the Cordillera, such power did not validate a discourse of legal rights and property relations, as it did in Europe.' 2003 précis (p. 138, read) and 2004 abstract: the management of dispossession by 'disciplinary technologies'. In-period readers. Loo (1998, read): the HBC's power was 'what Harris, following Michel Foucault, calls "sovereign power"', and 'the resettlement of British Columbia turned on "disciplinary power,"' which in British Columbia 'rested on the land system' (p. 65); the book 'is shaped by his reading of a diverse and complex international theoretical literature on power' (p. 64). Napoleon (2004, p. 114, read) names Foucault with Fanon, Said and Thompson. Qualification: Clayton (2003, p. 9, read) reports that Harris never '"lets theory loose" in British Columbia, as he puts it (xvii)'. The 1991 'Power, Modernity, and Historical Geography' (Annals of the AAG), which Clayton lists among his methodological essays (p. 6 n. 3), is unread.

named_group_routes.relationship: Gender and race in the making of a would-be white settler colony: British Columbia, 1849–71, where colonization and immigration were meant to produce a white, respectable society among a majority of Aboriginal people and failed to do so (2001), which she said was inspired by an international literature on gender and colonialism (no derivation from Wolfe's settler-colonial theory is established by the texts checked); later described by her as a comparative settler-colonial argument (2016)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own words, in period. 'Presence, Absence, and the Writing of BC History', BC Studies 132 (2001/02), pp. 57–64, read in full: On the Edge of Empire 'was initially inspired not by local experience but by a rich international literature on gender and colonialism. That through reading about imperialism elsewhere I came to see imperialism where I was is a suggestive comment on the convenient erasure of dispossession' (p. 58; the sentence ends 'settler consciousness' without a connecting word); 'The most remarkable pattern of silence probably concerns Aboriginal peoples' (p. 61). The 1995 essay (pp. 42–43, read) calls British Columbia 'a racially divided one controlled by a minority white population constantly engaged in a process of colonization' (p. 42). The book is unread; reviewers quote it: 'In contemporary newspapers and conversations, White British Columbians often long for the days when our society was unquestionably British … When we do so we long for a fiction of our own invention' (p. 201, as quoted by Carter, p. 117). In-period reviews. Sarah Carter, BC Studies 136 (2002/03), pp. 117–119, read in full: 'British Columbia fits within a broader context of European colonialism in that it was a settler colony where dispossesion [sic] of the indigenous societies and resettlement by a newcomer population were intertwined. While this is imperial history, it is not an example of the triumph of imperialism as in this era Aboriginal peoples remained demographically dominant and socially central' (p. 117); but 'The theme of the "social centrality and political agency" of the Aboriginal peoples of British Columbia could have been further developed' (p. 119). Myra Rutherdale, Labour/Le Travail 50 (2002), pp. 324–326, read in full: Perry shows 'how colonization and immigration worked in tandem in an attempt to create a White colony, while at the same time deliberately marginalizing the majority of the population, the Aboriginal peoples' (p. 325). Paul Orlowski, Left History 8:1 (2002), pp. 119–122, read in full: 'I found Perry's rendering of First Nations resistance to be lacking throughout much of the work, their portrayal emphasizing passivity rather than agency' (p. 121). Her own caution (1995, p. 43): 'my analysis minimizes the subjectivity of First Nations people'. No derivation from Wolfe is established by the texts checked: the 2001 essay cites Said, McClintock, Burton and Chakrabarty, not Wolfe, and the book is unread; the settler_colonialism roster already says Perry wrote 'earlier or beside' the paradigm. Later readings, labelled: in the BC Studies 190 forum (2016) she says the 2001 book 'makes the argument that British Columbia's history is best understood within a comparative framework of settler colonialism, echoing an assumption that undergirds Cole Harris's 1997 and 2002 books' (p. 112); Tony Ballantyne (2016, pp. 104–105) reads Colonial Relations (2015) as 'a salutary reminder of the limitations of work that follows Patrick Wolfe and Lorenzo Veracini in understanding "settler colonialism" as a fundamentally eliminationist project'.
named_group_routes.map_label: Gender, race and a settler colony, 1995–2001

named_group_routes.relationship: Fanon’s claim that colonialism shaped the colonizers as much as the colonized frames the question of how empire was lived “at home” (2002–2003)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Her own statement, read by the second research pass (JBS 42:4, 2003, p. 530): "Yet if, as Frantz Fanon argued, colonialism shaped the colonizers as much as the colonized then how was this expressed in everyday culture? How was it lived 'at home' as well as in the empire?" One explicit sentence framing the project; the Fanon text is not specified. Not to be confused with edge_418 (fanon → identity), which concerns Stuart Hall.

named_group_routes.relationship: Laura Lee Downs charges that Scott’s poststructuralist gender severs experience and subjectivity from the agency of the oppressed and treats discourse as “text-writ-large”; Scott replies that Downs misreads theory, which “analyzes how knowledge is produced” (1993)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: A named critic without a node, drawn from women's history, whose experience-and-agency tradition Downs defends. Downs (CSSH 35:2, 1993; p. 414 and the notes shown by the publisher read): Scott's book "has had an especially powerful impact upon historians, for it is through her eyes that many of us have become acquainted with post-structuralist thought"; "There is much to admire"; but it contains "a radical attack on the naïve suppositions of all previous feminist scholarship: a rejection of that ingenuous chain of reasoning which links subjectivity and experience to the hope that oppressed persons, too, might find some agency in history"; notes: "Scott treats discourse as text-writ-large". Scott's reply in the same issue (p. 438 read): "profound misapprehension"; "theory analyzes how knowledge is produced; theory does not produce either real life or practical politics." Distinct from Palmer (edge_920), Valverde (edge_967) and Canning (edge_702).

named_group_routes.relationship: Named critics within the debate beyond Palmer and Valverde, whose arrows exist: Stansell's worry about losing 'woman, the subject' (1987); Sangster's objection to 'the more radical, anti-materialist claims for deconstruction offered up by international scholars like Joan Scott' (2000); Eley and Nield's charge of an 'ungenerous critique' that allows 'either discourse … or materialist social history' (2000)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Scott's reply (ILWCH 32, p. 42, existing reading) reports Stansell's worry about losing 'woman, the subject'; Stansell's own p. 24 (existing reading) sides with Scott on poststructuralism while holding that social analysis of real women's activities is needed (editors' remarks, read). Sangster 2000 (read in full), pp. 157–158: the Canadian feminists kept 'materialist conceptions of work and the economy', 'unlike the more radical, anti-materialist claims for deconstruction offered up by international scholars like Joan Scott' (p. 157; her 'constructed as material' objection on the same page is aimed at Sewell, in Berlanstein's volume, not at Scott); 'The post-structuralist subject thus stands in direct contrast to the Thompsonian subject'. Eley and Nield's reply (2000, p. 83, read): 'we have some problems with Scott's ungenerous critique … It is either discourse (here signified by Jacques Rancière and Michel Foucault) or materialist social history'. Palmer's critique stays on edge_920 and Valverde's on edge_967; Downs (1993) is named in Scott's entry and not read here.

named_group_routes.relationship: Canadian debates included Palmer's materialist critique (1987–90), Valverde's sympathetic criticism of poststructuralist gender history (1990–95), Parr's gendered study of work (1990–95) and Sangster's materialist feminism (2000)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Sangster 2000, pp. 157–161 (read in full): the question 'whether we are simply replacing working-class history's failings concerning gender, with a linguistic approach that obscures class' (p. 157); Valverde cited for 'a certain logic carrying one from the (more generally accepted) deconstruction of notions of "male/female" skill to a complete deconstruction of class' (p. 158); 'Dismissing the "new" labour history as "mechanistic" marxism conflates diverse traditions of materialism' (p. 160 n. 121). Valverde 1990 (existing reading); Palmer's book through the Temple page and Callinicos. The existing strand cdn_working_class/state_of_the_field_2000 covers Palmer, Morton and Sangster from the Canadian field's side; this arrow records the debate's entry into it.

named_group_routes.relationship: A settler-colonial analytic worked out in conversation with Native American and Indigenous Studies: US Indian policy (removal, allotment, blood quantum, termination) read as successive modalities of elimination (2006, 2011); 'a key scholar in conceiving of a settler-colonial analytic in relation to Indigenous thinking' (Goeman, 2016)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Goeman 2016 (read in full): "a key scholar in conceiving of a settler-colonial analytic in relation to Indigenous thinking and scholarship that exists far longer than settler nations"; "He critically engaged our field in a respectful and nuanced manner". Kauanui 2016 (read in full), note 7: "his long time, direct intellectual engagement with scholars in Native American and Indigenous Studies", and para. 2: he insisted "that Native scholars did" create the field. Wolfe 2006 (read in full), sections on discovery and preemption, the Cherokee removal, allotment, blood quantum ("statistical extermination", quoting Jaimes) and termination; "After the Frontier" (2011) is unread. A contribution to the conversation, not an origin: the entry's Indigenous methods are not derived from him, and the dissent of Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel (2014) is recorded on the entry. Replaces the former comparison row. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

named_group_routes.relationship: Race as the outcome of 'differentiation, which is an intensely conflictual process' (2001): 'a race cannot be taken as given. It is made in the targeting'; Black people 'racialized as slaves', Indians eliminated 'as Indians' (2006); a comparative typology of colonial race regimes in Traces of History (2016)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Wolfe 2006 (read in full), opening section: "different racial regimes encode and reproduce the unequal relationships into which Europeans coerced the populations concerned"; "Black people's enslavement produced an inclusive taxonomy … For Indians, in stark contrast, non-Indian ancestry compromised their indigeneity"; "a race cannot be taken as given. It is made in the targeting"; and note 62 quoting his own 2001 essay, p. 894: "Difference … is not simply given. It is the outcome of differentiation, which is an intensely conflictual process." The 2001 essay is otherwise unread (Crossref: AHR 106:3, June 2001). Traces of History (2016) known through the British Library contents note (chapters on Australia, the United States, central Europe, Brazil, Palestine) and Veracini's obituary (read): it "utilises his analysis of racism under settler colonialism in order to explain racism everywhere else" and provides "a compelling typology of racial formations". Strengthens the entry-level comparison edge_885, which stays. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

named_group_routes.relationship: Settler colonialism set beside genocide studies: the Holocaust as 'the non-paradigmatic paradigm' against which 'qualified genocides' are devalued; 'structural genocide' proposed to retain settler colonialism's specificity without 'hierarchy among victims'; a chapter in Moses's Empire, Colony, Genocide (2006–08)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Wolfe 2006 (read in full): "Settler colonialism is inherently eliminatory but not invariably genocidal"; "The best known of all genocides was internal to Europe"; Lemkin's definition (note 6); Hull, Pohl, Zimmerer and "the modernity of colonialism"; "the Holocaust, the non-paradigmatic paradigm that, being the indispensable example, can never merely exemplify"; "the term 'structural genocide' avoids the questions of degree—and, therefore, of hierarchy among victims" (p. 403 per Kauanui). The 2008 chapter in Moses ed. is unread (Berghahn contents; Docker's "Are Settler-Colonies Inherently Genocidal?" in the same volume). The holocaust entry is historiographical; this compares frames and does not claim he wrote Holocaust history. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

named_group_routes.relationship: Settler against franchise colonialism: settler colonies 'were not primarily established to extract surplus value from indigenous labour' but 'premised on displacing indigenes from (or replacing them on) the land' (1999), 'a specific social formation' whose specificity is to be retained (2006)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Wolfe 1999, pp. 1–2 (existing reading, cpl129_wolfe_1999_intro: the introduction distinguishes settler from franchise colonies) and p. 3 as quoted by Englert 2020 (read): "In contrast to the kind of colonial formation that Cabral or Fanon confronted settler colonies were not primarily established to extract surplus value from indigenous labour. Rather, they are premised on displacing indigenes from (or replacing them on) the land". Wolfe 2006 (read in full): "settler colonialism is a specific social formation and it is desirable to retain that specificity". Englert finds the Fanon/Algeria example contradictory (Algeria depended on Indigenous labour). A comparison, not a critique: Hoxie 2008 (existing abstract) places the frame inside postcolonial critique, while Veracini's claim that postcolonial studies missed the settler situation is drawn at entry level (edge_882 revised). (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

named_group_routes.relationship: Treaties, preemption, removal and allotment read as 'the logic of elimination' rather than as relations and encounter: 'the murderous activities of the frontier rabble constitute [the colonial state's] principal means of expansion' (2006); set against the fur-trade historiography's 'middle ground', which Veracini records as a rival recovery (2013)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Wolfe 2006 (read in full), second section (the doctrine of discovery, preemption, the Cherokee removal: "The American right to buy always superseded the Indian right not to sell" (Rosenthal, quoted); "Rather than something separate from or running counter to the colonial state, the murderous activities of the frontier rabble constitute its principal means of expansion") and sixth section (allotment, blood quantum, termination). Veracini 2013, concluding section (author manuscript, read): "the recovery of a long lasting 'middle ground' between indigenous and settler polities in the past, sustained the possibility of renewed relationships"; "both the Canadian and US historiographies were late in adopting settler colonialism as a category of analysis". edge_869 already compares the two fields; this names the person's own reading. Canadian material is not his. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

named_group_routes.relationship: Wolfe took from Harris the sentence that 'the principal momentum of settler colonialism comes into focus' when capital's interest in uncluttered access to land is combined with settlers' interest in land as livelihood (2004, quoted 2006): a use as evidence, moderate
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Wolfe 2006 (read in full), third section and note 36, quoting Harris, "How Did Colonialism Dispossess?" (2004), p. 179: "Combine capital's interest in uncluttered access to land and settlers' interest in land as livelihood, and the principal momentum of settler colonialism comes into focus." Englert 2020 (read) also uses Harris 2004, p. 172, against Wolfe. The direction matters for edge_1014, which found no derivation of Harris from Wolfe: the citation runs the other way. A single quotation; influence in the sense of a use as evidence, as for locB_rel_26 in revision 1.152. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

named_group_routes.relationship: Critiques address both Wolfe's model and its subsequent uses: Macoun and Strakosch question structural inevitability; Rowse questions a teleology of elimination; Englert directly challenges elimination as the defining logic. Kauanui defends Wolfe against formulaic citation while rejecting the replacement of Indigenous Studies (2013–20)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Macoun and Strakosch 2013 (author version, read): "SCT can depict colonization as structurally inevitable"; "Foundational scholar Patrick Wolfe has been labelled 'very much a structuralist stuck in a poststructuralist world'"; "a kind of colonial fatalism"; "it does not account for Indigenous lives". Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel 2014 (read): "treating settler colonialism as a meta-structure, thus erasing both its contingency and the dynamics that co-constitute" it. Rowse 2014 (abstract, existing): a "teleology of elimination". Kauanui 2016 (read in full): a criticism of Wolfe's reception rather than of Wolfe, defending the theory against the phrase that 'often seems to stand-in for a serious engagement' with it, and asking that "Settler Colonial Studies does not, should not, and cannot replace Indigenous Studies". 'Wolfe and his Indigenous critics' is the citation graph's category for a co-citation pairing, not every author's declared position (Sol review 1.156, finding 3). Englert 2020 (read in full): "a critique of the Wolfe-an model"; elimination "does not accurately define the overall logic of settler colonialism, as claimed by Wolfe". Fairness: Kauanui and Goeman record his disclaimers and his engagement with NAIS; Macoun and Strakosch call his contribution "vital". (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

named_group_routes.relationship: Land as 'settler colonialism's specific, irreducible element': agriculture 'is inherently sedentary and, therefore, permanent' and 'progressively eats into Indigenous territory, a primitive accumulation that turns native flora and fauna into a dwindling resource' (Wolfe 2006); 'land is the irreducible element of settler colonialism' (Snelgrove et al. 2014)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Wolfe 2006 (read in full), fourth section: "Of itself, however, modernity cannot explain the insatiable dynamic whereby settler colonialism always needs more land. The answer that springs most readily to mind is agriculture"; "Agriculture not only supports the other sectors. It is inherently sedentary and, therefore, permanent"; "The reproach of nomadism renders the native removable." Snelgrove, Dhamoon and Corntassel 2014, p. 30 (read): "land is the irreducible element of settler colonialism, and … environmental degradation has often proceeded through and in support of settler colonialism". Tuck and Yang 2012, p. 5 (read): "Within settler colonialism, the most important concern is land/water/air/subterranean earth". The dissertation evidence for the pairing is in the entry's scope_note, not here. Drawn by Agent B by the coordinator's decision; Agent C does not duplicate it. (data/extension-2026/period4-wave1-2026-10-23/evidence-settler-colonial.md)

named_group_routes.relationship: Examines how British women’s struggles for prairie land combined gendered exclusion with unequal participation in Indigenous dispossession (Imperial Plots, 2016; read in corrected reprint 2018).
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Read introduction pp. 3–11, 19–23. P. 6 explicitly engages Wolfe, while pp. 9–10 qualify settler women’s privileges and complicity; the later pages explain cross-border and imperial scales. The source now exceeds the prior publisher-page-only evidence, whose wording and date remain in its verification history. This contribution concerns this specific later work; it neither assigns her entire earlier bibliography to one paradigm nor asserts an influence relationship from the citation alone.

named_group_routes.relationship: Uses conquest as a historical case for examining attitudes toward other societies
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The three authored opening paragraphs of “The Morality of Conquest, ” printed 89, explicitly identify the conquest of Mexico and its texts as the case. This limited methodological connection does not assert the unread book’s full thesis or label Todorov a member of a later school.

named_group_routes.relationship: Challenges the assumption that remembering victimhood necessarily prevents violence
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own UNESCO essay distinguishes selective remembrance from ethical use and warns that former victims can become aggressors. This is his bounded intervention on public memory, not a psychological finding or a universal judgment on victims.

named_group_routes.relationship: Wolfe explicitly agrees that frontier closure marks a major change, interpreting the post-frontier shift through Indigenous containment and assimilation within continuing settler colonialism (2013).
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Primary 257–259, especially 258, and 276 n 19. Qualified agreement is not blanket defense or proved influence. This remains an undirected comparison/reception link; Native sovereignty and continuing elimination remain central to Wolfe’s different account.

named_group_routes.relationship: Sangster questions Valverde’s suggestion that women’s history is not self-sufficient, reading it as implying gender history’s superiority (1996).
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The attribution is explicit in p. 240 n3; this records Sangster’s reading, not an agreed hierarchy.

named_group_routes.relationship: Gilroy identifies Du Bois’s double consciousness as a central organizing resource for his inquiry into the Black Atlantic.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The Black Atlantic, preface p. x, visually checked after OCR reading of ix–xi. This is Gilroy’s explicit acknowledgment, not an inference from a subtitle. Chapter 4 and the Du Bois originals were not reread; the book’s provisional, anti-closure framework and scant treatment of Fanon and James remain qualified.

named_group_routes.relationship: As Gonzalez, Modzelewski, Panich and Schneider explain, Wilson credits Fanon’s writing on decolonization with helping her articulate her own struggle in Reclaiming Our Humanity (2004).
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Explicitly mediated through the four named authors’ substantive 2006 account, read in an institutional repository. They also credit Paulo Freire’s work on praxis; his contribution is not reassigned to Fanon. Wilson’s original 2004 chapter remains unread here, and her family and community sources of knowledge retain their independent standing.

named_group_routes.relationship: As Deborah Simmons interprets his work, Adams draws on Fanon’s account of decolonization to connect autobiographical experiences of colonial alienation with collective historical struggle.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Explicitly mediated through Simmons’s 2002 tribute, pp. 6–7. Her reading connects Prison of Grass and Tortured People; their original and revised editions remain distinct. This is a specified intellectual resource, not an inference from Adams’s Marxist politics. The complete book bodies remain unread here.

named_group_routes.relationship: Byrnes and Coleborne identify Fanon as an intellectual resource for Walker’s counter-history of colonization and analysis of colonial power and resistance.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: This is the explicitly named reading of Giselle Byrnes and Catharine Coleborne in their joint 2011 editorial: p. 8 discusses colonial disavowal, and note 48 names the revised 2004 Ka Whawhai Tonu Mātou and Fanon’s The Wretched of the Earth and Black Skin, White Masks. Walker’s book and these Fanon editions were not freshly read. The 2004 witness is not silently backdated to the 1990 original or treated as the sole origin of Māori historiography.

named_group_routes.relationship: Pagden adopts Todorov’s contrast between Spanish initiative and Mexica efforts to maintain the status quo in his particular interpretation of the first sustained encounter, and acknowledges Todorov’s suggestions for improving his work.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Pagden’s introduction, p. lv and note 43, explicitly identifies Todorov’s point; acknowledgments p. vi credit Todorov alongside Richard Kagan and Ángel Delgado Gómez. This is a scoped use and named feedback, not endorsement of every part of Todorov’s conquest thesis or a general claim about Indigenous passivity. Hernán Cortés is the letters’ author; Pagden is translator, editor and introduction author; J. H. Elliott’s introductory essay is separate. Pages were read in the 2001 Yale Nota Bene edition of a work first published in 1971 and revised in 1986. The witness is not backdated to 1971, and the date of each introductory revision is not independently established. Todorov’s original book and the complete letters remain unread.

named_group_routes.relationship: Wolfe uses O’Brien’s evidence on New England treaty status and earlier blood-quantum practices in his history of Indigenous racialization and dispossession.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own fresh selected 2016 body and actual endnotes: chapter 5/n30 uses Firsting 203 for disadvantages facing tribes dispossessed before US treaty relationships; chapter 6/n92 uses Firsting 128 for an earlier Connecticut blood-quantum example. These are two specific resources within one pair/kind, not evidence that O’Brien endorsed Wolfe’s entire comparative framework. O’Brien’s cited pages remain unread in full; Wolfe’s original legal/historical sources are not independently checked. Ebook PDF pagination is explicit and not passed off as print pages.

named_group_routes.relationship: Includes Fanon in the political reading through which he developed his approach to Black self-determination and Marxist history.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Kelley’s answers describe reading Fanon in an All-African People’s Revolutionary Party study group, alongside Nkrumah, Ture, Cabral and Marx. The named-resources answer situates these readings in his effort to connect self-determination, political economy and more than material conditions. No particular Fanon title, formal teacher or exclusive influence is invented; original works unread.

named_group_routes.relationship: Reads Kahnawà:ke membership disputes as carrying 'the punctuating, juridical bestowals of settler colonialism', with status designations inscribed on persons (2007); refusal as 'an alternative to recognition politics in settler colonial society' (2017)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own words, 2007, p. 74; 2017 abstract (existing source, read). Nicoll (2015) quotes Mohawk Interruptus p. 3 on 'the structure of settlement that strangles their political form'. Wolfe appears in the 2007 article only as a supporting citation (n. 3); no critique of Wolfe is implied. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md)

named_group_routes.relationship: Finds at Kahnawà:ke no 'doubleness' of colonised consciousness of the kind 'that Fanon, Bhabha and Giddens speak of', but 'a tripleness, a quadrupleness' revealed at the point of refusal (2007)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own words, 2007, p. 74. Nicoll (2015, p. 56, read) independently reports that 'Simpson distinguishes this refusal from Fanonian "double consciousness"'. A qualified critique of one concept, not of Fanon's work as a whole. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md)

named_group_routes.relationship: Coulthard uses Fanon's critique of Hegel's master–slave dialectic against liberal recognition, while holding that Fanon's self-recognition 'fails to push us far enough' in settler states (2009)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own words, dissertation pp. 25–27 (Fanon used against Hegel and liberal recognition) and p. 159: Fanon's notion of self-recognition 'remains an innovative and important contribution', but he was 'less willing to explore the role that these forms might play in providing substantive alternatives'. Influence with explicit qualification. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md) Locators corrected in revision 1.204 to the printed page numbers of the UVic PDF (rechecked 2026-10-28, data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-B.md).

named_group_routes.relationship: Defines colonial domination as power 'structured' to 'facilitate the dispossession of Indigenous peoples of their land and self-determining authority': 'Canada is no different than any other settler-colonial power' (2009); 'territorially acquisitive in perpetuity' (2014)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own words, dissertation p. 10, and p. 37: 'Canadian settler-colonialism remains structurally oriented around achieving the same colonial effect it sought in the pre-1969 period: the dispossession of Indigenous peoples of their lands and self-determining authority'; the 2014 book p. 125 as quoted by Englert (2020, read). Wolfe and Veracini are not cited anywhere in the dissertation (full-text search, 2026-10-28); for the settler-colony frame he cites Abele and Stasiulis, 'Canada as a “White Settler Colony”' (1989), at p. 18 n. 47; Englert's own critique of Wolfe is Englert's, not Coulthard's. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md) Locators corrected in revision 1.204 to the printed page numbers of the UVic PDF (rechecked 2026-10-28, data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-B.md).

named_group_routes.relationship: Kauanui lists Trask's essay on 'settlers of color' in Hawaiʻi (written 1992; published in Amerasia, 2000) among analyses of settler colonialism that preceded Wolfe's (2016)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Named reader: Kauanui 2016, note 7 (reread 2026-10-27; the earlier project reading was in full). Trask's essay itself is unread. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-histories-2026-10-27/evidence-indigenous-authored.md)

named_group_routes.relationship: With Denise Henning (2021), Wheeler adopts Wolfe's definition: in the Americas 'classic colonialism evolved into settler colonialism', whose goal 'is the erasure of Indigenous peoples in order to establish settler rights to Indigenous lands and resources (Wolfe, 2006)'.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Henning and Wheeler, New Directions for Student Services 2020, nos. 171–172 (online 30 April 2021), section 'Colonization and intergenerational trauma' (early-view p. 3; print pp. 57–67); Wolfe 2006 (Journal of Genocide Research 8:4) in the references. A co-authored study (Henning first author) of rural Indigenous students' postsecondary experience: it uses the frame as historical context and does not discuss settler colonial studies as a field. Her earlier colonial analysis used Blauner's colonial model (1998) and postcolonial and anti-colonial theory (2000, 2010), without settler-colonial vocabulary.

named_group_routes.relationship: Postcolonial studies as an internal challenge to conventional history that opens space for Indigenous history: Wheeler draws on Fanon and Memmi to name 'intellectual colonialism', the colonization of Indigenous histories (2000), and counts 'critical and post-/anti-colonial scholars' among her teachers (2010).
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Stevenson [Wheeler], Decolonizing Tribal Histories (PhD, UC Berkeley, 2000), p. 79 ('The imposition of eurocentric categories on Indigenous knowledge of the past amounts to intellectual colonialism'), p. 80 (Fanon quoted on colonialism's distortion of the past), pp. 117–118 (section 'Postcolonial Studies': Fanon and Memmi, with examples 'relevant to issues of Indigenous history … to demonstrate the value of postcolonial studies'); pages read through OCR. Wheeler 2010, p. 48.

named_group_routes.relationship: Coulthard reads Adams as the writer Fanon 'most influenced' and takes from him that Indigenous 'cultural self-empowerment can be captured or co-opted by the state apparatus and directed toward neo-colonial ends' (2009)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Coulthard's dissertation (2009), pp. 188–194 (read): p. 188, Fanon 'most influenced the work of the late … historian and Red Power activist Howard Adams'; p. 193, 'There are a number of insights to be gleaned from Adams' engagement with the work of Fanon', first the co-optation quoted above, which he applies to the 1970s Dene movement; p. 194, Adams's call to revive traditions that empower and discard those that oppress, applied to Indigenous women's struggle against the Indian Act's patriarchal legacy. The biographical and autobiographical passages on pp. 188–190 are not used (OCAP). Whether the 2014 book keeps this reading is unchecked. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-B.md)

named_group_routes.relationship: Takes Fanon and Memmi as 'the classic sources' on internalised colonisation, while noting that The Wretched of the Earth does not treat Native North Americans (1999)
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own words, 1999 dissertation (read 2026-10-28): PDF p. 48, 'Frantz Fanon and Albert Memmi are the classic sources for discussion on the processes of internalization'; PDF p. 12, classic (Fanon, Memmi) and contemporary works 'have convincingly shown that colonization produces a pervasive structural and psychological relationship between the colonizer and the colonized'; PDF p. 40 (qualification), 'Frantz Fanon in Wretched of the Earth does not deal with the treatment of Native North Americans either'. Parallel to edge_2140 (Said). Memmi has no node. (data/extension-2026/indigenous-edge-review-2026-10-28/review-C.md)

named_group_routes.relationship: Wolfe uses Jacobson’s formulation of republican inclusion and racial/gender exclusion as interdependent to develop his account of race and colonial power.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own Wolfe 2001, 875/n29 quotes Jacobson 22–23 while discussing Morgan’s slavery/freedom analysis; Morgan and David Brion Davis retain separate substantive credit. Wolfe adds a specific reservation about Jacobson’s treatment of liberalism, and 893/n100 includes him among resources for the historical expansion of whiteness while preserving differences from anti-Black racialization. Positive use coexists with the separate qualification; original Jacobson 22–23 not freshly read, so the quotation’s mediation through Wolfe is explicit.

named_group_routes.relationship: Wolfe qualifies Jacobson’s account of republican inclusion and exclusion for leaving liberalism’s own credentials insufficiently interrogated.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own 875/n29 explicitly attaches this limited reservation to his otherwise substantive quotation of Whiteness 22–23. This is a brief, scoped critical qualification, not an extended refutation of Jacobson’s book or a claim he ignored all relations of power. Wolfe’s positive use remains separately represented; his 893/n100 distinction among racial regimes is not falsely treated as refuting Jacobson’s own 9 warning against equating experiences. Original Jacobson 22–23 remains unread here.

named_group_routes.relationship: Invokes Wolfe’s call for a unified historical field while arguing that representation and material consequences should be studied together (2003).
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own introduction 10–11 explicitly uses Wolfe in defending the combination of political, administrative, military, social and cultural history. This does not automatically classify the book as adopting every settler-colonial model. Note 28’s body and the Wolfe original are unread; exact title or edition not invented.

named_group_routes.relationship: Todorov credits Barthes’s receptive teaching and intellectual exchanges with amplifying students’ ideas during his early French literary formation.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own1997P11 describes admiration, theoretical humility and active improvement of students’ ideas, not merely thesis supervision. P15 says Barthes’s works played an important role while distinguishing Todorov’s later truth-regulated dialogue from what he thinks Barthes would share. Genette/Bremond/Metz network retains shared credit. Spanish interview rendering/translator unestablished; no complete Barthes originals read.

named_group_routes.relationship: Todorov recalls Lévi-Strauss’s clear rational argument and movement between detailed analysis and bold generalization as an admired model in his structuralist formation.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own 2001 reply in 2003 translated sample footer 8 praises precisely these qualities while saying personal contact was rare and kinship/myth studies differed from his literary interests. It also qualifies later scientific ambitions and relativism. Admired intellectual model, not direct mentorship, wholesale allegiance or claim all remembered reading was contemporaneous. La Pensée sauvage 1962/Anthropologie structurale 1958 identified by notes 13–14, original bodies unread.

named_group_routes.relationship: Todorov questions Lévi-Strauss’s sweeping scientific ambitions and some claims about cultural relativism and the subject, while retaining admiration for his analytical reasoning.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own translated retrospective footer 8 explicitly recalls a critical study later included in Nous et les autres and states that peremptory claims seemed to exceed Lévi-Strauss’s own best thought. Not a report that Lévi-Strauss replied: Todorov says there was no reaction. Exact underlying chapter and full original anthropological works unread. Source is 2001 interview/2003 Spanish edition, not a falsely contemporaneous 1960s objection.

named_group_routes.relationship: Todorov identifies Weber’s ideal types and analyses as attractive resources within his renewed study of political philosophy for Nous et les autres.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own1997P21 distinguishes useful reading from agreement with every author. It names Strauss’s natural-right dispute and Aron’s introduction as surrounding interpretive mediation, then explicitly states attraction to Weber’s ideal types/analyses. Max Weber, not Eugen Weber. Cited original works unread; no assertion all political-philosophical reading had one source or first-reading date.

named_group_routes.relationship: Todorov resists Weber’s agonistic account of war and the ultimate incompatibility of values, preferring dialogue and a horizon of universality.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own1997P21 directly qualifies his appreciation of ideal types and describes the disputed stance as Weber’s Nietzscheanism. This is Todorov’s interpretation, not independent verification that it exhausts Weber. Strauss/Aron debate contextual mediation retained; originals unread and no invented direct exchange.

named_group_routes.relationship: Todorov questions the coherence between Derrida’s democratic commitments and deconstruction’s treatment of values, while acknowledging the theory’s internal sophistication.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own1997P25 explicitly locates his objection between public ethical commitments and professional philosophy, not an internal logical refutation. Blanchot’s anti-value statement supplies a separate example, not a quote assigned to Derrida. P27 retains friendship/intellectual admiration but says Derrida did not answer his philosophical interests. Spanish rendering; underlying Derrida/Blanchot texts unread.

named_group_routes.relationship: Todorov adapts Arendt’s banality-of-evil argument when explaining his own emphasis on ordinary acts of good rather than exceptional heroism.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own 1997 P37 explicitly calls his banality of good similar and contrary to Arendt’s argument yet grounded in the same reasons; conceptual adaptation, not simple disagreement or denial of evil. P21 separately names Arendt among a plural philosophical education without implying full agreement. Eichmann book and full Facing Extreme originals unread; interviewer’s framing distinguished.

named_group_routes.relationship: Todorov challenges Horkheimer and Adorno’s pessimistic Enlightenment narrative for treating a real but avoidable historical development as if it had to culminate in totalitarianism.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Actual own answer in opening 2016 interview, published 2020, names both coauthors; Horkheimer lacks endpoint but shared responsibility retained. Todorov concedes shadows and potential threats of Enlightenment, so this is not denial of its destructive uses. Only displayed opening read; original Dialectic and rest of interview unread. Precise question supplied instead of fabricated page.

named_group_routes.relationship: Leichter reports Ricœur’s approving use of Todorov’s warning that claims to victim status can generate demands on others, within Ricœur’s distinction between justice for other victims and self-victimization.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Explicitly named 2012 scholarly mediation 124–125/nn68–69 directs to English Memory, History, Forgetting 86. Neither Ricœur’s original French 2000 nor Blamey/Pellauer 2004 English body nor original Todorov warning freshly read. This scoped quotation/use is not broad agreement on every duty-of-memory issue, and does not make Leichter an original formative source.

named_group_routes.relationship: Todorov describes introducing Russian Formalist approaches into French literary debate through his 1965 translated anthology and subsequent editorial work with Jakobson.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own1997P13–15 details translation/selection, Genette’s editorial introduction, Sollers/Pleynet’s publication role and Jakobson’s advice/preface;2001 interviewsample6–7 describes continued editing/translation assistance. Scoped contribution to linguistic literary inquiry, not membership in every poststructuralist position. Later dialogical/ethical departure and criticism of deconstruction retained; no generic biography-based route.

named_group_routes.relationship: Todorov criticises Lacan’s opaque and seductive style as contrary to his own ethical commitment to clarity, rational argument and readers’ capacity to answer.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own translated retrospective sample8–9 explicitly states this intellectual and communicative objection. The personal encounter is his recollection, not independent proof of Lacan’s psychology; the claim is limited to Todorov’s criticism of style and intellectual authority. He distinguishes his sustained interest in Freud and admiration for Lévi-Strauss from his response to Lacan. Full Lacan texts unread.

named_group_routes.relationship: Todorov credits reading Habermas, among several interlocutors, with his renewed education in political philosophy for Nous et les autres.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own1997P21 explicitly describes these authors as a second university and identifies Habermas/Aron with a Kantian universalist orientation. This is a plural, qualified reading resource rather than allegiance to every position or a claim of personal contact. Arendt, Strauss, Berlin, Aron and Bénichou retain their distinct roles; no full Habermas original freshly read.

named_group_routes.relationship: Trouillot draws on Todorov when distinguishing historical truth claims from fiction and fabrication.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own5/n2 and6–8/n5 use LesMoralesdelhistoire1991,129–169;157/n1 includes it among works helping chart a route between positivist and constructivist poles. Later79/n9 uses Todorov on rights of man/citizen. Selected manifestations and scope, not sole intellectual origin or fresh reading of Todorov’s book.

named_group_routes.relationship: Trouillot acknowledges The Eighteenth Brumaire among works informing his route beyond one-sided accounts of historicity.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own 157/n1 explicitly includes Marx with Chesnaux/Ferro/de Certeau/Cohen/Guha/Pomian/Schaff/Todorov, with influence not always registered by mechanical citations; 1926 English manifestation listed. Daut 2021, 135–144 specifically warns against reducing his Haitian intellectual genealogy to Marx. This narrow acknowledgment neither establishes exclusive inspiration nor makes Haitian political analysis dependent on a European source.

named_group_routes.relationship: Deloria uses Todorov’s analysis of Spanish colonial discourse as a resource in mapping critical histories of conquest and represented Indigenous difference.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own 2002 10 places Todorov The Conquest of America 1984 WITH Benjamin Keen 1971 in the Spanish part of his conquest/discourse historiography and characterizes Todorov moralist literary-critical. Exact cited edition 23 The Question of the Other, translated Richard Howard, New York Harper Row 1984; not 1982 French original fresh reading. Named historiographical resource, not mentorship or adoption of all Todorov. B frozen Todorov 12 no pair, reserved here.

named_group_routes.relationship: Carter uses Wolfe’s logic-of-elimination framework when interpreting the dispossession and exclusion underlying prairie homesteading.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Imperial Plots 6/note 6 explicitly names Wolfe and applies the formulation within her analysis of land, reserves and excluded Indigenous farmers. The note cites his 2006 Journal of Genocide Research article, 387; the bibliography supplies 387–409. The article remains unread in this dossier. This is a bounded resource in the 2016 book, read in its corrected 2018 reprint, not an influence inferred from citation alone or a retrospective classification of all Carter’s earlier work. Earlier edge_1315 retains its limits.

named_group_routes.relationship: Greer adopts Wolfe’s critique of naturalized settler history and continuing dispossession while seeking a more differentiated colonial chronology.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own 2019:62–63 explicitly calls for taking on board Wolfe’s historiographical critique, developed further by Veracini, and values the structure-not-event formulation. Notes 2–3 and 7–8 distinguish Wolfe 2007,1999,2006 and Veracini 2010; originals remain unread here. Positive uptake coexists with Greer’s scope objection; neither automatic full agreement nor a direct personal teaching relationship is inferred.

named_group_routes.relationship: Greer argues that Wolfe’s settlement–exploitation dyad needs extension to capture other overlapping colonial forms in northern North America.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own 2019:63–64 names Wolfe’s Australia/India focus, then introduces imperial/commercial penetration and extractivism as additional modes. Greer insists these coexist and overlap rather than form self-contained stages. He expressly values Wolfe’s critique and does not attribute every casual temporal flattening to Wolfe himself. Existing group critique edge_1012 remains; original Wolfe texts are unread.

named_group_routes.relationship: Valverde explicitly places her work in Foucault’s tradition of developing theoretical tools through concrete historical research.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own What Counts as Theory, Today? (2016), 174 and178, expressly identifies her Foucauldian working tradition and uses power/knowledge to explain how jurisdiction assigns different forms of governance. Her adoption of Bakhtin is explicitly an additional resource rather than abandonment of Foucault, while she rejects automatic eclecticism. This is a qualified intellectual debt stated in2016, not a first-publication date for her1991method or a claim that all her work derives from one thinker. Existing group route858 retains its broader moral-regulation context; original Foucault works are not newly read.

named_group_routes.relationship: Valverde uses Derrida’s Spectres of Marx to challenge the opposition between theoretical sophistication and politically engaged labour history.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own Deconstructive Marxism (1995),332–338, calls the book a resource for rethinking the theory/politics and ideal/material oppositions, while preserving Marx’s emancipatory project and the importance of historical inheritance. Her339–340 discussion explicitly stops short of Derrida’s undeconstructible justice and expresses reservations about its mystical context. The specific positive resource coexists with her earlier critique of Scott967; it is not a blanket endorsement, proof of personal contact or a new reading of Derrida’s original or Peggy Kamuf’s1994translation. Lorna Weir’s explicitly acknowledged help with deconstruction remains separate.

named_group_routes.relationship: McKay challenges the extension of Valverde’s Toronto–Ottawa evidence into an undifferentiated English Canada while praising her methodological innovation.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own A Note on Region (2000), 92–93 and note 3, names The Age of Light, Soap and Water and questions its spatial scale, regional typicality and use of a part to stand for a whole. He calls the book pioneering and deserving of praise for its methodology, while suggesting that a Boston–Halifax axis might be more pertinent for some Atlantic questions. This is a specific geographical and historiographical objection, not rejection of moral regulation or a new reading of Valverde’s complete book. The article lightly edits an unpresented 1997 talk and is dated by its 2000 publication; Valverde’s earlier work is not treated as responding to McKay’s later framework.

named_group_routes.relationship: Wolfe adapts Mauss’s total social phenomenon to analyse anthropology as a total discursive practice participating in colonial settlement.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own 1999 introduction 3 explicitly identifies the adaptation, while note 6 quotes Mauss 1925 [1970]:1 on simultaneously religious, legal, moral, economic, aesthetic and morphological institutions. Wolfe treats anthropological debates as primary data rather than adjudicating their claims about Indigenous life. This is a particular methodological resource, not equivalence between the two complete projects or a newly read Mauss original; bracketed 1970 does not become first publication.

named_group_routes.relationship: Wolfe uses Spivak’s distinction between exposing mechanisms and making individuals speak to explain his refusal of ethnographic ventriloquism.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own introduction 4 invokes Spivak 1988:288 while distinguishing the analysis of anthropological constructions from an attempt to recuperate an allegedly pristine Indigenous voice behind them. Political and empirical methodological limits converge in his argument. This records his explicit use of a particular distinction, not proof he adopted all of Spivak’s work, a claim Indigenous people had no voice, or a newly read Spivak original; the cited original title is not guessed.

named_group_routes.relationship: Chakrabarty supervised and commented on the entire doctoral draft from which substantial portions of Wolfe’s first book developed.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own acknowledgments vii distinguish three successive supervisors, Maurice Bloch, Greg Dening and finally Chakrabarty; the last read and commented on the whole draft. This is specific critical scholarly input to the thesis, not a claim he alone formed Wolfe or read the final 1999 book. Wolfe explicitly separates the later rewritten book and the whole-book readings by Phillip Darby and Michele Grossman. No particular adopted revision or common theoretical doctrine is invented.

named_group_routes.relationship: Higginbotham uses Williams’s account of language as continual creation to support her analysis of racial language appropriated for resistance.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Own 270/note 57 cites Marxism and Literature,31, at the point where she explains Black appropriation of productive linguistic power. Bakhtin’s double-voiced discourse and Fanon’s cultural self-recovery retain their separate roles. This particular conceptual support does not establish complete adoption of cultural materialism; original 1977 book unread.

named_group_routes.relationship: Chukwudinma and Kallon trace Rodney’s early use of Fanon’s analysis of the national bourgeoisie when interpreting Tanzania’s socialist experiment.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: Named scholarly readers Chukwudinma and Kallon 2025 explicitly identify The Pitfalls of National Consciousness as Rodney’s frequently invoked resource during 1969–74 and afterwards. They quote his 1972 accounts of the dependent petty bourgeoisie and intelligentsia’s possible transformation, while distinguishing his terminology from Fanon’s and crediting Cabral for a class-suicide formulation Rodney associated with Fanon. The authors show later revision and continuing debt rather than an unchanging or exclusive lineage. This is their attributed analysis of quoted published and archival Rodney material; the original papers, full lectures and Fanon book remain unread.

named_group_routes.relationship: Chukwudinma and Kallon identify Rodney’s later disagreements with Fanon over revolutionary organization and the class character of postcolonial African societies.
named_group_routes.evidence_note: The authors’ 2025 original article quotes Rodney’s 1973 Cabral eulogy and 1978 Hamburg distinction between violence itself and its political organization, then traces his post-1974 view of Tanzania’s bureaucracy as a ruling class rooted in production. They describe a move beyond the early model of a dependent stratum that might renounce privilege. Their account expressly calls Rodney’s portrayal of Fanon as an apostle of spontaneity a misreading, since Fanon also demanded organization; it also finds that Rodney retained some Fanonian hopes about guerrilla leadership. The disagreement is Rodney’s interpretation as mediated by these two readers, not a finding that Fanon simply ignored organization or a complete rejection of Fanon. Original eulogy, recordings, research papers and Fanon book unread. The existing James 401 criticism concerns a distinct retrospective assessment of Rodney.

coverage.other_missing_hold_name_screen: Exact normalized full-person labels checked across all33 continuation dossiers. Other matching mixed hold lists explicitly retain existing edges, unread originals or insufficient specificity; only the Fanon false absence requires a new claim here. Todorov clarification is evidentiary, not an automatic edge.

proposals.relationship: Wolfe questions the reach of Fanon’s labor-dependent colonial schema in settler formations organized around Indigenous land displacement.
proposals.evidence_note: Own 1999 Introduction 1–3, actual licensed publisher preview, with printed 1 and 3 visually collated. Wolfe contrasts settlers’ relative immunity to withdrawal of Indigenous labor with Fanon’s master–slave schema, citing Fanon 1967:47 and 28. He credits material grounds for optimism in particular African contexts of the 1960s and discusses Cabral alongside Fanon without equating their analyses. This is Wolfe’s qualified reading of a colonial model, not a universal rejection of Fanon or a verified description of all African or Algerian formations. The original Fanon and Cabral texts remain unread. Existing group comparison edge 1234 preserves Englert’s specific objection to Wolfe’s treatment of Fanon and Algeria; this addition does not adjudicate that disagreement.

cpl129_wolfe_1999_intro.note: Separately reviewed coverage correction: actual original 1999 Introduction 1–3 independently read again, with 1 and 3 visually collated. The qualified Fanon labor-dependent schema criticism is specific enough for the existing full Fanon endpoint; a previous missing-endpoint hold was mistaken. Cabral co-context and African contextual optimism remain explicit. Original Fanon/Cabral works unread; Englert’s separate Algeria objection retained without adjudication.

preservation: All frozen dossiers/reviews, stable IDs and existing graph records preserved, except this approved append-only source note. This is a correction to a completed dossier, not another historian completion.
